v: The Father himself, who sent me, has testified about me. You have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his form.
You don’t have his word living in you, because you don’t believe him whom he sent.
b: This passage is Jesus' most direct, most searching, and saddest exposure of the religious leaders. He points out that these men, who considered themselves well versed in the Law, looked devout on the outside and had the Scriptures memorized, yet had never truly known God.
Here Jesus gives three serious but true diagnoses: they had not heard God's voice, they had not seen His form, and they had not kept His word abiding in their hearts.
Why? Because they did not believe in Jesus, the One the Father sent. To reject the Son is to reject the Father; to refuse Jesus is never to truly know God.
1. The Father Himself has testified about Jesus (v. 37a)
Jesus said, “The Father who sent me, he has testified about me.”
The Father's testimony is not hidden. It is clear, public, and continuous:
• At Jesus' baptism, the Father opened the heavens and said, “This is my beloved Son.”
• In Jesus' miracles, the Father confirmed Him with power.
• In His teaching, the Father confirmed Him with wisdom.
• In His cross, the Father confirmed Him with redemption.
• In His resurrection, the Father confirmed Him with eternity.

The Father has declared Jesus' identity countless times and in countless ways. Yet the religious leaders still could not see or hear. It was not that God had not spoken; it was that they were unwilling to listen.
2. They had never heard God's voice or seen His form (v. 37b)
Jesus said, “You have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his form.”
This statement is astonishing.
They thought they understood God best, were the most devout, and knew the Bible most thoroughly. But Jesus said: you have never come to know God.
They read the Law but did not know the Lord of the Law; they kept the Sabbath but did not meet the Lord of the Sabbath; they knew the Scriptures but did not meet the One to whom the Scriptures point.
This is the greatest tragedy of religion: outwardly full of devotion, inwardly far from God.
God's voice is not heard with the ears but with the heart. God's form is not seen with the eyes but with a spiritual life.
If a person's heart is not open to God, he can hear a thousand sermons and still not hear God's voice; he can read the Scriptures a hundred times and still not see God's form.
3. The heart of their problem: God's word was not in them (v. 38)
“You don't have his word living in you.”
The original says it “does not remain in you,” meaning God's word had not taken root, had not stayed, and had not grown into life.
They kept the Scriptures in their heads but not in their hearts. They memorized the Law but did not submit to the God the Law reveals.
And what was the evidence? Jesus said, “because you don't believe him whom he sent.”
Faith is the one sure sign that God's word is in the heart. If a person truly receives God's word, he will receive the One God sent. Rejecting Jesus proves that God's word is not in his heart.
This also reminds us:
Unbelief in Jesus is not a matter of “not enough information” but of “an unwilling heart.” It is not that the mind cannot understand; it is that the heart will not receive.
Faith is an open heart; unbelief is a closed heart.
4. What this passage reminds us
1. Religion can look splendid on the outside, but if the heart is not open to Jesus, we will never meet God.
2. True spiritual life is being able to hear God's voice and see God's work.
3. If God's word is not in the heart, no amount of reading or listening will help.
4. Believing in Jesus is the only proof that the heart has truly welcomed God.
Jesus is not merely rebuking here; His heart is calling out. May people turn back, may they receive the truth, and may they no longer stay in outward devotion while passing by the living God.
q: Do you keep God's word in your head, or in your heart?
Today, where is Jesus calling you to open up more deeply and store His word in your heart?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, we ask that our hearts would not only hear Your word, but let Your word dwell in us. May we not be devout only on the outside, but truly know You, see You, hear You, and follow You. Remove from us all refusal, stubbornness, and closedness, so that we may open ourselves completely to receive Your Son Jesus. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: “You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me.
Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life.
b: These two verses are among the most penetrating truths in John's Gospel, and the deepest sigh Jesus ever gave over religious people. The words sound gentle, but they act like a surgeon's scalpel from the Holy Spirit, cutting open the deepest blind spot in a person's life:
A person can be extremely familiar with the Bible and yet completely miss Jesus. A person can zealously search for truth and yet be unwilling to come to the One who is the Truth.
This passage was not only spoken to the Pharisees of that day; it is a reminder to every one of us who follow Christ.
1. They searched the Scriptures, but wrongly thought the Scriptures themselves held eternal life (v. 39)
Jesus said, “You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life.”
Notice that He is not criticizing Bible study; He is criticizing a mistaken expectation.
They thought—
• the Scriptures were eternal life itself
• knowing the Scriptures well could save them
• mastering the text was the same as possessing life
But Jesus said: the Scriptures are not life itself; the Scriptures are a signpost that guides people to life.
The Scriptures are not the destination; they are the road. They are not the source; they are the witness. The Scriptures do not save; they point to the One who can.
Like a hand pointing to the moon, the hand is not the moon; like a sign pointing toward home, the sign is not home.
If we grasp the finger rather than the direction it points, we will never reach the destination.
What the Scriptures point to is Jesus. Jesus said, “these are they which testify about me.”
Moses, the prophets, the Psalms, the Law—all say one thing: “Christ is coming.”
If a person holds on to the Scriptures but misses Jesus, it is like memorizing the map and never setting out.
2. Jesus' deepest sigh: you will not come to me (v. 40)
He said, “yet you will not come to me, that you may have life.”
It is not that they cannot see; they will not.
It is not that they do not understand; they do not want to.
It is not that they are unable; they are unwilling.
They pursued knowledge but refused life; they loved research but would not open up; they embraced the Scriptures but rejected the Lord to whom the Scriptures testify.
Jesus' heart is grieved—He longs to give life, but people are unwilling to come.
Notice that Jesus did not say, “You cannot come.” He said, “You will not come.”
Life is not blocked; it is refused.
The door is open, but people will not enter.
Jesus' invitation is not to join a course, a Bible study class, or a religious activity. His invitation is: come to me.
Life is not in the Bible itself; life is in the One the Bible points to—Jesus.
3. What this passage reminds us of
1. Bible study cannot replace being close to Jesus.
The Scriptures are the road, not the end.
2. Knowledge cannot replace life.
The more knowledge we have, the more humility we need.
3. Spiritual activity cannot replace a spiritual relationship.
Outward diligence is not the same as an open heart.
4. The purpose of reading the Bible is not to gain information but to meet Jesus.
Every page says to us: “Come to the Lord.”
5. Rejecting Jesus is not always open rebellion; it can be the gentle refusal of “not being willing to open up.”
Being busy, not wanting to repent, and not being willing to submit are all ways of “not being willing.”
Jesus' heart is simple yet deep: “It is good that you study the Scriptures, but please come to me to have life.”
This is not a rebuke; it is an invitation, an opening, a longing, a call of love.
q: When you study the Scriptures, is it for more knowledge or to meet Jesus?
Today, are you willing to “go to Him” more deeply?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, keep us from reading the Bible merely for knowledge, but to meet Jesus. May we not only study Your word, but truly open ourselves and be willing to come to Jesus for life. Take away from us every unwilling, resistant, and closed heart, so that we hunger for You and draw near to You, and life may flow from You. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: I don’t receive glory from men.
But I know you, that you don’t have God’s love in yourselves.
b: These two verses are extremely short, yet like a sharp sword they pierce straight into the depths of the heart. Jesus did not beat around the bush. He saw through the hearts of the religious people and pointed to the root of their failure: not a lack of knowledge, not a lack of effort, but no love of God in their hearts.
These two verses also uncover two things that matter most for our spiritual lives:
1. Are we following human glory or God's will?
2. Is the love of God really in our hearts?
1. Jesus said, “I don't receive glory from men” (v. 41)
Jesus' life had no need at all of human applause. He did not live on praise, nor did He depend on people's approval. His worth did not come from the crowd but from the Father.
He did not seek fame, position, or influence; He sought one thing only—that the Father's will be done.
This statement also reflects the greatest difference between Him and the religious leaders:
The religious leaders
• cared about people's opinions
• cared about people's evaluations
• sought people's respect
• feared people's eyes
Jesus
• cared only about the Father's heart
• sought only the Father's glory
• was not moved by people's applause
• was not moved by people's criticism or judgment
When He said this, it was clear and firm; His focus was not on people at all, but on the Father.
This is a life emptied of self. It is not pleasing people but pleasing God; not seeking people's approval but seeking God's delight.
If our faith only wants to protect our face, our image, and our reputation, we can never truly follow Jesus.
2. Jesus discerns the heart: “you don't have God's love in yourselves” (v. 42)
This statement is startling. He did not say: “You don't understand the Scriptures.” “You haven't performed the religious rituals well.” “You need to change your behavior.”
He said: the root of the problem is that you do not have God's love in your hearts.
Notice He did not say, “You don't know how to love God.” He said, “You don't have God's love in yourselves.”
It means: God's love has not entered your hearts, has not touched you, has not changed you, has not warmed you, and has not made you surrender to Him from within.
You have knowledge, tradition, ritual, and outward devotion, but inwardly you have not been conquered by God's love.
A person can memorize the Bible, keep the rules, perform the rituals, and attend the meetings, yet not have God's love.
This is Jesus' deepest sorrow. They replaced a relationship with God by religious activity, replaced love by rules, and replaced knowing God by knowledge.
What is the result of having no love of God in the heart?
• Being unable to know Jesus (because without loving God, one cannot love the Son)
• Being unable to obey the truth (because obedience comes not from pressure but from love)
• Being unable to live out life (because life flows out of love)
• Being left with only a religious appearance (because there is no real connection with God)
• Easily seeking human glory (because there is no Father's love in the heart to satisfy)
Religion may look lively, but if the heart has no love, it is empty.
Jesus saw not behavior but the heart. He did not say, “You haven't done enough.” He said, “Your hearts are not filled with God's love.”
This is not condemnation; it is an invitation—to let God's love dwell again in our hearts.
3. Two important lessons this passage reminds us of
1. Do not live in glory that comes from people.
That turns our faith into a performance rather than life. Let us follow Jesus' example and fix our focus on the Father's eyes.
2. Let God's love dwell in your heart.
The root of spiritual life is not knowledge but love; not effort but being loved; not pressure but surrender. If God's love does not enter our hearts, our faith will become mere religion.
Let God's love move in, and we will truly know Jesus, long for Jesus, and follow Jesus.
q: What are you doing today to seek people's approval rather than God's delight?
Are you willing to ask the Father to fill you with His love, so that your heart is truly open to Jesus?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, give us the heart of Jesus, so that we no longer seek the glory of men but seek Your delight. Fill our hearts with Your love, so that we are not devout only outwardly but renewed inwardly by Your love. May Your love dwell in us, so that from the heart we know You, obey You, and love You. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: I have come in my Father’s name, and you don’t receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him.
b: This verse opens up a very deep truth about human nature and exposes the greatest blind spot of religious people: people often reject what comes from God while welcoming what comes from man. They reject the truth but accept words that flatter them. They reject Jesus but accept voices that suit their taste.
This is Jesus' heaviest charge against the religious leaders of His day, and it is a deep reminder for us today.
1. Jesus came in the Father's name, yet was not received
Jesus said, “I have come in my Father's name, and you don't receive me.”
He did not come with His own authority, to build His own power, or to win people's favor.
He came in the Father's name, carrying the Father's will, to complete the Father's commission.
Behind everything He did, every word He spoke, and every decision He made was the Father's heart.
But—the religious leaders did not receive Him.
Why?
Not because He was not clear enough, not because He was not wise enough, not because He lacked miracles, not because His preaching fell short, not because He was not holy enough.

It was because He did not fit their expectations. His words were too real and pricked the heart; His light was too bright and showed up the darkness; His authority was too direct and broke tradition; His grace was too free and went beyond their frameworks.
They rejected Jesus not because He was wrong but because He was too right.
He came to expose the human heart, and the human heart fears nothing more than facing the truth.
2. If another comes in his own name, they will receive him
Jesus said, “If another comes in his own name, you will receive him.”
This statement pierces the entire religious system.
The meaning of the original is: as long as someone speaks as you like, caters to your taste, and meets your expectations, you will receive him.
The human heart always prefers—
• people who make me comfortable
• people who match my expectations
• people who say what I want to hear
• people who don't hurt me, challenge me, or discipline me
• people who let me feel that I don't need to change

These are those who come “in their own name.” They do not come for God but for themselves. They do not lead people to repent but make people comfortable. They do not point out the truth but promote themselves.
Religious people reject the truth yet welcome false prophets; they reject the light yet accept flattery; they reject Jesus yet accept voices that demand no change, only outward piety.
This is not an ancient problem; it is the most common phenomenon in churches, among believers, and in society today.
3. Why does the human heart reject Jesus and accept people?
The reasons are simple:
1\. Jesus demands true repentance
Repentance requires admitting wrong, opening the heart, and laying down self. This is what people least want to face.
2\. Jesus' light exposes darkness
When the light shines, no one can hide. People would often rather stay in the dark than face the light.
3\. Jesus' truth demands a changed life, not a changed appearance
Religious activity is easy; a change of heart is hardest.
4\. Jesus tears down human pride and self-centeredness
He said, “If anyone wants to follow me, let him deny himself.” The cross of self-denial is what people least want to carry.
5\. Human eyes favor those who cater to them
People like to control, hold power, and be affirmed. But Jesus calls us to surrender, humility, and following.
If the human heart is not changed, it will always find it easy to reject God and accept people.
4. Three reminders this passage gives us
1. Do not accept only the truth that suits your taste.
True truth often challenges me, disciplines me, and changes me.
2. Do not measure what Jesus says by “what I like.”
Jesus did not come to please me; He came to save me from myself.
3. Teach your heart to welcome Jesus, not the voices that cater to me.
Sometimes the voice that loves us most is the one that stings us most.
Jesus' words never flatter, and His words always bring life.
May we not reject Jesus as the Pharisees did, but open our hearts to welcome His truth.
q: Lately in your life, has Jesus challenged you and called you with the truth?
Are you willing to lay down the voices of people and choose to receive Him?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, help us not to reject Jesus and follow those who cater to us. Give us wisdom to discern what is Your voice and what is the voice of man, so that our hearts long for Jesus, receive Jesus, and obey Jesus. If Your truth must sting us, give us courage to open ourselves to You. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: How can you believe, who receive glory from one another, and you don’t seek the glory that comes from the only God?
b: This verse is like a bright beam shining into the deepest motives of the human heart. Here Jesus points out the root obstacle to believing in Him: not the intellect, not the truth, not the evidence, but—the pride in a person's heart and the longing to please one another.
He reveals the true reason people reject Him: not that they do not know, but that they are unwilling; not that they do not understand, but that in their hearts they love the glory of men more.
This verse brings three very deep revelations.
1. Receiving glory from one another: the spiritual trap people fall into most easily
Jesus said, “you who receive glory from one another.”

The meaning of the original is: you praise one another, affirm one another, and seek one another's approval, measuring spiritual worth by people's applause, people's evaluation, people's eyes, and people's standards.
What the religious leaders valued most among themselves was:
• who was honored as a teacher
• whose authority was greater
• whose title was higher
• whose interpretation was most popular
• whose status was most affirmed
• who best fit the group's expectations
Their hearts were not before God but before people. They did not want to please God but to please people. They did not long for God's glory but for the applause of their peers.
“Receiving glory from one another” is a trade in spiritual appearances: I affirm you, and you affirm me; I praise you, and you praise me; within the same framework we satisfy each other's pride.
This false spiritual peace is the greatest enemy of faith.
2. Not seeking the glory that comes from the only God
Jesus said their problem was not mainly “seeking glory” but “seeking the wrong glory.”

If the heart does not seek God's glory, it will naturally seek glory from people. The two cannot be pursued at the same time. Once the heart longs for people to “see me, affirm me, like me,” it is hard to simply seek God's pleasure.
God's glory is—
• God's affirmation
• God's applause
• God's delight in my life
• God saying, “You are my beloved child”
• God's will fulfilled in me
Human glory is—
• whether I perform well
• whether others like me
• whether they respect me
• whether my rating is high
• whether my position matters
Jesus said: you pursue the glory of men, not the glory of God.
A person whose heart cares about human glory is always pulled around by outside forces; a person whose heart seeks God's glory becomes freer and freer.
3. Jesus said: how can you believe?
This statement is not a rebuke but a revelation.

His meaning is: “As long as your heart still cares about people's eyes, you will reject me. Because following me requires self-denial, humility, and surrender, and human glory is always the opposite of these.”
In other words: human glory suffocates faith.
• Caring about people's eyes, we will fear Jesus' truth.
• Caring about people's applause, we will reject Jesus' challenge.
• Wanting to save face, we cannot carry the cross.
• Wanting to keep up our image, we cannot truly surrender.
• Wanting to please people, we cannot fully trust Jesus.
This is the Lord Jesus' reminder to believers of every generation: a heart that seeks human glory cannot lay hold of Jesus at the same time.
Faith needs a simple heart—one that only wants to be seen by God and does not care how people see it.
4. The deep reminders this verse gives us
1. The deepest idol of the human heart is not money but “what others think of me.”
This keeps faith at the level of appearance rather than reality.
2. If we care more about people's applause, we will fear the truth of Jesus piercing us.
The Lord often prunes us through truth, but we often fear what people will think.
3. To trust in Jesus, we must first lay down human glory.
Lay down face, lay down image, lay down self-respect, lay down people's expectations.
4. True freedom is no longer being bound by people's eyes and wanting only to please God.
Jesus' question is a reminder of love: “How can you believe?” He is not rejecting us but inviting us—inviting us to turn our hearts from people's applause back to God's glory.
q: Today, what is there that you still care about in people's eyes, so that you dare not fully obey Jesus?
Will you ask God to help you turn your heart from human glory back to His glory?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, cleanse our hearts so that we no longer seek the glory that comes from men but seek Your delight. Remove our fear of people's eyes, our dependence on applause, and our craving for approval. Make our hearts simple and pure, wanting only to please You. Let us be truly free to believe in Jesus and follow Jesus. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: “Don’t think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you, even Moses, on whom you have set your hope.
b: These words are Jesus' most startling reminder to the religious leaders, and a deep warning to those who have the outward form of religion without real life. He did not accuse them, nor did He charge them before the Father; but He pointed out that what truly accuses them is neither He nor the devil, but the very Law of Moses they lean on, are confident in, and depend on.
This verse points to three crucial spiritual truths.
1. Jesus is not the accuser but the Savior
Jesus said, “Don't think that I will accuse you to the Father.”
This is not a disclaimer but a statement of His heart. He is not a judge on the bench accusing people; He came not to condemn but to save.
John 3:17 says, “For God didn't send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him.”

Jesus is not an accusing voice; He is a voice that calls, restores, heals, and renews. He is not like the religious leaders, quick to rebuke, accuse, despise, and judge; He is humble, gentle, and full of compassion.
He has no desire to accuse anyone; He invites every person to return to the Father's embrace.
If someone is finally condemned before God, it is not because Jesus accused him, but because he rejected Jesus' salvation.
2. What truly accuses them is the Law of Moses they rely on
Jesus said, “There is one who accuses you, even Moses, on whom you have set your hope.”

This is very deep. What the religious leaders were proudest of was the Law of Moses. They boasted that they understood the Law, kept the Law, taught the Law, and made spiritual judgments based on the Law.
They thought Moses stood on their side, but Jesus said: “The one who accuses you is Moses.”
Why?
Because the Law is meant to point to Christ, not to exalt human righteousness. The Law does not prove “I am good”; the Law leads people to admit “I need a Savior.”
Romans 3:20 says, “for through the law comes the knowledge of sin.”
The Law is like a mirror that lets people see their own filth, not something to show off one's cleanness.
But the religious people used the Law as a tool to glorify themselves, and so they were accused by the Law itself.
The more they boasted in the Law, the more the Law proved their debt. The more they tried to stand by the Law, the more the Law exposed their true condition.
What truly accuses people is not Jesus but the self-righteousness they rely on.
3. Why the Law accuses: because the Law points to Christ, and they rejected Him
Moses not only gave the Law, he also prophesied the Prophet who was to come—Christ (Deuteronomy 18:15).
The whole Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms point to Jesus. But the religious leaders:
• agreed with the Law but rejected the Jesus to whom the Law points
• boasted of keeping the Law but rebelled against its true meaning
• were confident in knowing Moses but rejected the Christ Moses proclaimed
It is like someone holding a map and bragging that he has taken the right road, yet never arriving at the map's destination.
The Law was never the end; Jesus is.
So when a person rejects Jesus, the Law he relies on becomes his accuser. For to reject Christ is to reject the heart of the Law.
In other words:
What the Law accuses is not behavior but a heart that rejects Christ.
4. Important reminders this passage gives us
1. Jesus is not one who comes to accuse but one who comes to save.
If we hear an accusing voice, it is not from Him.
2. Self-righteousness puts a person under the judgment of the Law.
The higher the self-confidence, the harder the fall; the more one relies on himself, the less he can receive Christ.
3. The Law is a road, not the goal; the goal is always Jesus.
If Bible reading, service, devotion, and conduct do not lead us to love Jesus more, they become a witness against us.
4. True freedom is moving from the Law to Christ.
The Law shows our need; Christ meets our need.
May we boast not in religion but in Jesus; may we stand not by works but by grace.
q: Is your faith built on your own conduct and performance, or on the grace of Jesus?
Are you willing to let the Law lead you to Christ rather than remain in self-righteousness?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You are not a God who accuses but a God who saves. Take away our self-righteousness, so that we do not rely on our own works but rely on the grace of Jesus alone. Teach us not to stay in the outward form of religion, but let the Law lead us to lean on You more deeply, to long for You, and to draw near to You. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote about me.
b: This verse is Jesus' call, extremely gentle yet full of authority. He does not deny Moses but affirms him; He is not against the Law but fulfills it; He does not mean to discard the Old Testament but to unveil its true core.
He lets the religious people understand: whoever truly understands Moses will surely meet Jesus. Whoever truly believes the Law will surely walk toward Christ.
For everything Moses wrote was preparation for Him.
1. Whoever truly believes Moses will surely believe Jesus
Jesus said, “For if you believed Moses, you would believe me.”
His meaning is not “you need to try harder” but “you have never truly believed Moses.”
The religious people had memorized Moses' words but had not lived out Moses' heart.
They knew the letter of the Law but did not believe in the Messiah to whom the Law points.
They boasted of being Moses' disciples, but their lives were already far, far from Moses' faith.
In Moses' heart, what mattered most was not the Law but the promise
Moses' whole life was spent waiting for the Savior who was to come.
• In Genesis, the woman's offspring would bruise the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15)
• Abraham's offspring would become a blessing to all nations (Genesis 22:18)
• The sacrificial system that foreshadowed Christ (Leviticus)
• The Passover lamb that foreshadowed redemption (Exodus 12)
• The rock in the wilderness giving water (1 Corinthians 10:4 says that rock was Christ)
• The bronze serpent lifted up so that people might be saved (John 3:14–15)
• Moses said with his own mouth, “Yahweh your God will raise up for you a prophet from among you, of your brothers, like me; to him you shall listen” (Deuteronomy 18:15)
Every part of Moses' teaching points to one thing: the Messiah is coming.
So Jesus said, “If you truly believed Moses, you would believe me.”
In other words—those who do not believe Jesus have not truly believed Moses either.
2. At the core, what Moses wrote points to Christ
Jesus said, “for he wrote about me.”
The whole Pentateuch, from beginning to end, bears witness to Jesus. He is not an added character; He is the protagonist of the whole Bible.
The world of Moses' writing is a complete portrait of Christ
1. Genesis—He is the Lord of creation, the woman's offspring, the seed of Abraham
2. Exodus—He is the Passover lamb, the redemption, the true Moses
3. Leviticus—He is the priest, the sacrifice, the tabernacle, the atoning blood
4. Numbers—He is the rock in the wilderness, the pillar of cloud and fire, the victorious leader
5. Deuteronomy—He is the Prophet who is to come, the fulfiller of the Law
Everything Moses wrote is not a story of law but a story of redemption; not a religious textbook but a blueprint of Christ.
If Moses himself stood up, he would say: “Don't look at me; look at Christ. Everything I wrote testifies about Him.”
3. The religious people's problem was not that they did not understand the Bible, but that they would not believe Jesus
Jesus did not say they had not read Moses; He said:
Your hearts are not open, so you cannot see me.
The religious people's problem was not a lack of knowledge but a closed heart.
They read the Scriptures but did not seek God; they studied but would not submit; they were zealous but did not love God; they knew the Law but rejected the heart of the Law.
What truly kept them from believing Jesus was not reason but pride—a heart unwilling to admit its need of a Savior.
And the whole of Moses' life was to guide people to admit their need and to point to Jesus, the only One who can save.
4. Reminders this verse gives us
1. The purpose of the Bible is not knowledge but to bring us to meet Jesus.
If reading the Bible does not lead us to love Jesus more, we are only stopping at the letter.
2. True faith begins with an open heart, not with understanding in the head.
The more the head knows, if the heart does not submit, the harder it becomes.
3. The Old Testament is not religious history but the foretelling and foreshadowing of Christ.
In reading the Old Testament we must see Jesus, or we will become slaves of the Law like the Pharisees.
4. Self-righteousness is the greatest reason we fail to see Christ.
Moses points out sin so that we may come to Jesus for forgiveness and life.
May we not, like the religious people, stop at the letter, but meet Jesus, long for Jesus, and obey Jesus whenever we read the Bible.
q: Lately, has your Bible reading brought you closer to Jesus, or has it stayed at knowledge?
Will you ask God to open your heart so that every time you read, you meet Him?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for making the whole Bible point to Jesus, so that we are not lost in the Law but are led to the Savior. Open our hearts to You, so that we not only understand the letter but meet life. May we love Jesus more the more we read, be humbler the more we study, and surrender more the more we know. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: But if you don’t believe his writings, how will you believe my words?”
b: This verse is Jesus' last word in chapter five, like a clear yet weighty voice pointing to the religious people's deepest blind spot, the core question of the whole conversation, and the most basic reason people reject Jesus:
Not a lack of knowledge but a heart that does not believe. Not that they cannot understand the Bible but that they are unwilling to obey it. Not a lack of evidence but a refusal of the truth itself.
Here Jesus' words seem to sum up the message of the whole chapter and touch the deepest question in a person's life—reading the Scriptures yet not believing the One the Scriptures call us to believe.
1. Jesus said: you read Moses but do not believe Moses
He said, “But if you don't believe his writings…”
The religious people did not fail to read Moses; they read Moses thoroughly, studied him, taught him, and recited him.
But Jesus said they “do not believe Moses.”
Why?
Because those who truly believe Moses will see that Moses' writings keep saying:
The Messiah is coming, the Savior is coming, Christ is coming.
Every law, every feast, every foreshadowing, and every deliverance Moses recorded was meant to point to that One—Christ.
But the religious leaders turned the Scriptures into:
• a tool of self-righteousness
• a weapon to accuse people
• a badge displaying spiritual status
• a religious prop to prove their own greatness
They experienced the letter but did not meet the life behind the letter.
So Jesus said, “You do not believe Moses.”
Not because they did not read, but because they did not obey.
Not because they did not understand, but because they did not open up.
True faith is not agreement of the mind but surrender of the heart to God.
2. If you do not believe Moses' writings, you cannot believe my words
Jesus said, “how will you believe my words?”
His meaning is: “If you do not receive the truth in the Scriptures that points to me, you cannot receive me, the Truth Himself.”
Believing in Jesus is not an isolated act; believing in Jesus is the climax, the core, and the purpose of the whole Bible.
The whole Old Testament is the stage, and Christ is the protagonist.
The whole Law is the shadow, and Christ is the substance.
All the foreshadowings are signposts, and Christ is the Way itself.
If we deny the true meaning of Moses, we cannot receive Jesus.
If we reject Moses' preparation for Christ, we cannot see Jesus' glory.
The religious people rejected Jesus not because the evidence was lacking but because the door of their hearts was shut.
If the heart is not open, no amount of evidence will help
Just as, if the window is shut, the brightest sunlight cannot shine in.
If the heart is not open to God, no amount of truth can get in.
Jesus did not lack evidence; people lacked a heart willing to believe.
3. What this passage reminds us
These words were not spoken only to the religious leaders; they are also spoken to everyone today who is willing to follow Jesus.
1\. Reading the Bible is not the goal; meeting Jesus is the goal.
If we read the Bible without loving the Lord more, drawing closer to the Lord, or being more willing to obey the Lord, we are only reading words, not reading life.
2\. Knowledge cannot bring faith; an open heart can.
Faith is not understanding in the head but a response of the heart. If the heart is not open, knowledge only becomes pride.
3\. Refusing to obey, we lose the ability to know God.
The religious people were not unable to understand; they were unwilling to obey. Without willingness to obey, there will be no belief.
4\. The focus of the whole Bible is Jesus.
If we read the Bible and do not see Jesus, it means we have not yet understood.
Jesus is not a theme added onto the Bible; He is its core, its center, and its fulfillment.
5\. The barrier to faith is not external but internal.
What truly keeps people from believing Jesus is not circumstances, reason, or hard questions, but the pride, self, refusal, and closedness in the heart.
If the heart is willing to open, God's word can come in, and the light of Jesus will shine.
4. Jesus' words carry a gentle call
Although He points out their unbelief, there is no condemnation in His tone, only an invitation of love:
“Will you open your heart to believe? Will you let Moses lead you to me?”
He does not mean to push people down; He means to bring people back to the Father.
q: When you read the Bible, do you let it bring you to Jesus?
Today, are you willing to say to the Lord, “Lord, I am willing to open my heart and believe You”?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for giving us the Bible, so that we can see the beauty of Jesus. Keep us from stopping at the letter, but lead us into life; not to stop at knowledge, but to enter into faith. Open our hearts, so that as we read Your word we meet Jesus and respond to Your voice with our lives. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: After these things, Jesus went away to the other side of the sea of Galilee, which is also called the Sea of Tiberias.
b: This verse looks like a simple narrative. There is no miracle, no teaching, no conflict, no dialogue, yet it is the starting point of the whole chapter's miracles and teaching and holds deep spiritual meaning.
Sometimes God's most important leading is hidden in what looks like an “ordinary step.” And that step is often the key by which He opens the next stage of grace for us.
1. After these things: God's work in our lives is continuous
The text begins: “After these things.”
“These things” refers to the Sabbath dispute in chapter five, the Jews' persecution of Jesus, and Jesus' teaching and unveiling.
That was a tense time, with conflict, questioning, persecution, and rejection all in it.
Yet the text says—“After these things,” Jesus was not bound by the conflict or stopped by the criticism; He moved forward step by step, continuing to walk in the Father's way.
God's work is not interrupted by circumstances; God's plan does not stop because of human opposition.
Sometimes we think circumstances have disrupted our spiritual journey, but in God's eyes there is no disruption, only advance.
After conflict comes a new step; after rejection comes a new opening; where people close, God turns to another place.
“After these things” reminds us: there is no chance in life, only God's leading.
2. Jesus crosses the Sea of Galilee: God often brings us across into a new scene
“Jesus went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee”
This is not ordinary movement; it is a symbolic “crossing over.”
The Sea of Galilee is often used as a symbol of:
• the boundary of life
• God's new work
• the beginning of a new spiritual stage
• the meeting place of human limitation and God's limitlessness
Jesus was not going around in circles; He was bringing the disciples into a new realm, preparing for the next greater miracle—the five loaves and two fish.
Every crossing of Jesus is an opportunity for the disciples' lives to grow.
Today God also often brings us across: across old thoughts, old comfort zones, old limits, old fears, old patterns.
He often leads us away from the “known” toward the “unknown,” so that we may experience His provision and reality.
The Sea of Galilee was a place the disciples knew well but could not control, and also a place where God often showed His glory.
God often brings us into territory that is “familiar but not under my control,” to teach us to trust Him.
3. The Sea of Tiberias: God still reigns within human territory
The text adds: “which is the Sea of Tiberias.”
This name was given to the Sea of Galilee by Greeks and Romans, symbolizing Gentile culture, political power, and territory controlled by men.
It means: in places that seem to belong to the world, God still reigns; in settings that seem unspiritual, Jesus still works wonders.
God works not only in the temple but also in the secular; He is present not only on the Sabbath but also in people's daily lives.

One side of the Sea of Galilee was Jewish territory and the other the Gentile world. Jesus crossed not only a lake but a boundary—bringing the kingdom of God to the most ordinary corners of the world.
This gives us great hope:
Do you feel your workplace is “not a spiritual place”? Your family “not very godly”? Your daily setting “very worldly”?
Take heart: Jesus is willing to enter the territory of the Sea of Tiberias; He is willing to enter every part of your life.
4. Life reminders this verse gives us
1. God's leading continues “after these things.”
No interruption, no accident; His hand has always been ahead.
2. Every crossing is the beginning of new grace.
Before the Sea of Galilee were the five loaves and two fish; before your crossing there is also God's preparation.
3. Even in what looks like “human territory,” Jesus still holds the royal authority.
Do not limit God to the church; He will show His glory in your daily life.
4. An ordinary verse may be the starting point of God's great work.
One seemingly simple line, “went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee,” is the prelude to feeding five thousand.
God is often preparing a “great work” in the “small step” we think is nothing special.
q: Is there a “Sea of Galilee” in your life right now that needs crossing?
Are you willing to believe that God is preparing grace for the other side of that crossing?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for leading us across every step in our lives. Let us believe that “after these things” You still reign, and that on the road we cross You have already prepared grace. Lead us bravely out of our comfort zones into the new season You have prepared for us. May we see Jesus' presence and work in every part of our lives. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: A great multitude followed him, because they saw his signs which he did on those who were sick.
b: This verse looks simple, but it actually reveals the human heart, faith, and our motives for following the Lord. It is the central groundwork of the whole chapter and lays important foreshadowing for the miracle of the five loaves and two fish.
On the surface it looks like a good thing—many people were following Jesus. But Jesus' aim was not “many followers”; what He cared about was: why were these people following Him?
This short verse shows us three deep spiritual truths.
1. Many people followed Jesus, but not every following was the right following
The text says, “A great multitude followed him.”
A crowd is not faith; a multitude is not disciples; excitement is not life; outward following is not inward following.
In Jesus' ministry, those who followed Him were often of three kinds:
1. Those who came because they saw miracles (seeking blessings)
2. Those who came because they heard His words (seeking truth)
3. Those who were willing to take up the cross and follow Him (true disciples)
The first kind was the largest and the third the smallest. Even later in chapter six, many of those who had been following Him “went back, and walked no more with him” (John 6:66).
Why? Because true following is not watching the spectacle but facing the truth, obeying the truth, and loving the Lord who speaks the truth.
Following Jesus is not walking behind Him on the outside but surrendering to Him on the inside.
2. Their reason for following Jesus: because they saw miracles
“because they saw his signs which he did on those who were sick.”
They followed not because of who Jesus was but because of what Jesus did.
They longed for power, healing, solutions to problems, benefits, help, and an exciting atmosphere. The focus of their following was not Jesus Himself but what Jesus could “do for me.”

This is “blessing-seeking following”—wanting only grace and not the cost; wanting only to see miracles and not to hear the truth; wanting only problems solved and not life surrendered; wanting only healing and not the cross; wanting only benefits and not lordship.
Jesus does not refuse people's needs; He had compassion on the sick and healed them. But if people stop at the level of “miracles,” they can never truly know Him.
A miracle is a signpost, not the destination. The destination is not healing itself; the destination is the Healer.
After the miracle of the five loaves and two fish, Jesus said to this crowd:
“You seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves, and were filled.” (John 6:26)
They saw the deed but could not see God's heart. They pursued benefits and missed life.
3. Through this crowd Jesus reveals the tendencies of the human heart
This verse not only records the people of that time but also reflects us today.
We too are often like this crowd—
• we pray to solve problems, not to meet Jesus
• we read the Bible to be blessed, not to gain life
• we go to church to feel comfortable, not to have our hearts changed
• we follow Jesus to get help, not to let Him be King
• we look for miracles more than for God's will
• we seek grace more than we seek the Lord's face
When Jesus blesses us we draw near; when Jesus challenges us we draw back. This is the psychology of the crowd, not the life of a disciple.
True faith is not “because I saw a miracle.”
True faith is “because He is Lord.”
True following is not “because He satisfies me” but “because He is worthy of my following.”
This verse reminds us: our reason for following Jesus decides whether we can go the distance.
4. Life reminders this verse gives us
1. Following Jesus cannot stop at miracles; we need to enter into truth.
Miracles attract our eyes, but truth renews our hearts.
2. The focus of following the Lord is not getting blessings but getting the Lord Himself.
Miracles pass; Jesus never changes.
3. If we seek only help and not lordship, we will fall quickly.
The crowd follows fast and also leaves fast.
4. True faith is choosing to follow even when we see no miracle.
For the foundation of faith is not experience but the reality of Jesus.
q: What is your reason for following Jesus?
Today, are you willing to say to the Lord, “Lord, I follow You not for miracles, but because You are my Lord”?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, cleanse our motives for following Jesus, so that we follow You not for blessings but because of Your love and truth. Help us to seek not only miracles but You Yourself. Let our hearts surrender more deeply and long more deeply, so that Jesus becomes the focus and goal of our following. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Jesus went up into the mountain, and he sat there with his disciples.
b: This verse again has no miracle, no teaching, no dispute, yet it holds deep spiritual meaning. It is the prelude to the miracle of the five loaves and two fish and also unveils the principle behind Jesus' ministry.
One action of Jesus—going up on the mountain. One choice of Jesus—sitting with His disciples. These two simple descriptions are the core rhythm of His whole life of ministry.
He was not driven by needs; He was not tied down by crowds; He was always led by the Father.
Let us see in this verse three beautiful spiritual practices of Jesus.
1. Jesus went up on the mountain: He chose to leave the crowd and align with the Father
The text says, “Jesus went up into the mountain.”
Going up the mountain means leaving the noise, the crowds, the pressure, the needs, and the expectations, and entering the Father's mind, the Father's presence, and the Father's guidance.
In the Bible, Jesus often went up on the mountain:
• going up the mountain to pray (Luke 6:12)
• going up the mountain to be transfigured (Matthew 17:1)
• going up the mountain to teach His disciples (Matthew 5:1)
• going up to face temptation (Matthew 4, set on the heights of the wilderness)
Jesus' ministry rhythm was always: first go up the mountain, then come down; first meet the Father, then meet people; first gain strength in quiet, then serve among the crowds.
Even the Son of God needed to go up the mountain; how much more do we.
Many times it is not that the circumstances are too busy but that the heart is too busy. It is not that time is too short but that the focus is wrong.
Jesus going up the mountain says: “I will not let needs decide my direction; I will let only the Father's voice guide me.”
Going up the mountain is not escape but focus.
On the mountain He heard the Father's voice; below the mountain He completed the Father's work.
Without time on the mountain, we will be spent below. Without aligning with the Father, we turn ministry into pressure rather than grace.
2. Jesus sat down with His disciples: He shepherded His disciples first rather than satisfying the crowd first
“and he sat there with his disciples.”
This sentence is full of warmth.
Jesus was not standing to preach, not rushing about doing things, not busy arranging the next step. He “sat down,” which means rest, calm, relationship, and companionship.
And He was not sitting alone; He sat “with His disciples.” The priority is clear:
He shepherded the disciples first, then faced the crowd.
Jesus valued relationship over ministry, disciples over crowds, life over results, the inside over the outside.
The miracle of the five loaves and two fish happened after Jesus first was quiet, first was with, and first taught His disciples.
Jesus is never in a hurry; He always acts on the Father's timing. He is not anxious or rushed; His sitting down expresses the peace and certainty in His heart.
This reminds us: if service makes us busier, more tense, and with less relationship, it is not Jesus' rhythm.
Jesus' rhythm is: sitting down—rest; together—one heart; there—the Lord works wherever He is
3. Jesus “there”: God often works in “places we think are ordinary”
The text says, “and he sat there with his disciples.”
No city, no temple, no stage, no lights, only “there.”
Yet the miracle of the five loaves and two fish—a miracle that has touched generations and is recorded in all the Gospels—began “there.”
God often does not work in places we think are “special” but in places we think are “ordinary.”
On the mountain—an ordinary place; sitting down—an ordinary posture; talking, being together—ordinary moments
Yet the prelude to the miracle was in them.
To God there is no “ordinary,” only “where He is.”
As long as Jesus sits there, that place becomes where the Father works.
4. Life reminders this verse gives us
1. We need to go up the mountain to be quiet and let our lives first align with God.
It is not that we pray after we finish being busy, but that prayer gives us strength to be busy.
2. Be with people in relationship first, then begin ministry.
Jesus' ministry always begins with “sitting together,” not with “being busy.”
3. God often works in very ordinary moments.
In any “there,” Jesus can begin wonders.
4. Jesus' rhythm is rest, not tension.
He sat down because He knew the Father reigns.
May we also enter Jesus' rhythm, not rushing on our own but led by the Holy Spirit; not hurrying to analyze with the mind but following the Lord with the heart.
q: Are you willing to have “going up the mountain” time every day—quiet, prayer, focus?
In your life, is there a “there” where Jesus is inviting you to sit down with Him?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, bring us into Jesus' rhythm, so that before the rush we align with You, before serving we learn quietness, and before acting we sit with You. Teach us to lay down our busy hearts, our own analysis and control, and listen to Your voice alone. May we walk with You in any “there” and experience Your work. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand.
Jesus therefore lifting up his eyes, and seeing that a great multitude was coming to him, said to Philip, “Where are we to buy bread, that these may eat?”
He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do.
b: This passage looks like a smooth narrative, yet it holds deep spiritual insight. The miracle of the five loaves and two fish did not happen suddenly; Jesus had already prepared it where the disciples could not see. Each of His steps was full of purpose, guidance, shepherding, and testing.

First, we see that the Passover was near. This was one of the most important feasts of the year, the great day when the people remembered God's redemption—the lamb's blood shed, God's hand stretched out to save, the people set free. In this very season that symbolized “God's provision and salvation,” Jesus was preparing to do a miracle about “food” and “life,” to let the people see once more: true provision comes from God, not from what human hands can calculate.

Next, Jesus lifted up His eyes and saw a great crowd coming. He did not wait for the problem to happen before dealing with it; He saw first, was moved first, and prepared first. The Lord's eyes are not cold but compassionate; not passive but actively seeking people's needs. Before the people had said a word, He had already lifted His eyes. This reminds us: when we feel a need approaching or a challenge closing in, the Lord has already seen it and already knows.

Then Jesus asked Philip, “Where are we to buy bread, that these may eat?” This was not seeking an answer but leading Philip into faith. Jesus did not lack a way; He was testing Philip's vision—do you look at the problem or at the Provider? Do you rely on calculation or on faith? Do you depend on your own ability or on the Lord who knows what He will do?

Philip's reaction (later he immediately calculates that two hundred denarii would be needed) shows our human habit—we always look first at what is lacking, at difficulty, at limits, and then panic. Jesus' test was not to shame him but to build him up. The Lord often uses seemingly impossible situations to teach the disciples: a problem is not an obstacle but a playground for faith; a trial is not a barrier but an opportunity to trust.

He Himself knew what He would do. This sentence is the heart of the whole passage. He was not improvising or thinking as He went. He fully knew the Father's plan and fully held the timing of every step. The disciples were anxious, but Jesus was at rest. The disciples counted the cost, but Jesus had already seen the outcome. He was not looking for a method; He Himself is the method.
This passage reminds us:

First, the seasons of our circumstances are not accidental; God has His purpose in them. When the Passover was near, God was about to show once more that He is the Provider. Every season in which you feel pressure rising may be a moment when God is about to do something new.
Second, Jesus always sees our needs first. Before we pray, He has already lifted His eyes; before we speak, He is already moved; before we understand, He already knows.

Third, a test is not for condemnation but for growth. When the Lord asked, “Where are we to buy bread?” He was not checking whether Philip understood but whether Philip was willing to learn to depend on Him.

Fourth, Jesus already knew what He would do. This sentence is enough to give faith rest. When we know nothing, cannot see the road, and feel the pressure, the Lord is not at a loss. He knows the method, the timing, and the road, and He also knows He will use this situation to shape us.
q: Does the challenge you are facing now make you, like Philip, see only what is lacking?
Today, are you willing to hand your problem over to the Lord who “knew what He would do”?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You have already seen when we cannot see clearly and already know when we do not know how. Teach us not to look first at the difficulty but first at Jesus; not to count resources first but first to trust Your provision. May we learn to depend on You in every test and believe that You know what You will do. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Philip answered him, “Two hundred denarii worth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may receive a little.”
One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him,
“There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are these among so many?”
b: This passage reveals the disciples' inner reactions when facing the “impossible.” Philip tried to understand the problem by calculation; Andrew weighed the resources by reason; a child simply gave the little he had to the Lord. Through the reactions of these three, Jesus unveils to us the deepest training of faith.
Philip saw “not enough,” Andrew saw “too little,” but the child gave “everything” to Jesus. The difference in faith lies in this—do we look at resources, or at the Lord?

First, look at Philip's reaction. He said, “Two hundred denarii worth of bread is not sufficient for them.” Philip responded to the problem in a rational, calculating, practical way. His answer was not wrong, but it showed that he kept his focus on visible possibilities rather than on Jesus' power. He had already concluded: “impossible.” Philip was a good man, but he represents that part of our lives that habitually calculates first and always sees limits first.
Philip's conclusion was: “It can't be done.” But what Jesus was actually leading him toward was not “how to do it” but “whom do you trust?”

Next, look at Andrew. He went one step further than Philip. He neither denied the problem nor ruled out the possibility. He found a boy and brought the five loaves and two fish he had to Jesus. But at the same time he said, “but what are these among so many?” Andrew did something good—he found a resource—but he still evaluated it with human eyes: “what are these?”

Sometimes we are like Andrew: we see a possibility, but are immediately doused by reality. We see a little hope, but our reason at once denies it. We see a little resource, but feel it is too trivial, even unworthy to be placed before God.
But the real turning point is in that child. He understood nothing, analyzed nothing, calculated nothing. He did only one thing: he gave everything to Jesus.
Five loaves and two fish were no feast and no rich resource, only a child's lunch for the day. But placed in Jesus' hands, they became the beginning of a miracle.
Miracles often begin not with “very big” but with “very small but willingly offered.”
Smallness is not the problem; unwillingness to offer is the problem.
God does not look at how many loaves there are; God looks at whether the heart is willing.

Just as the widow of Zarephath offered the last handful of flour (1 Kings 17), and that day she met the God who provides; the child offered the five loaves and two fish, and that day he saw with his own eyes thousands fed.
The Lord often does not ask, “How much do you have?” He asks, “How much are you willing to give Me?”
Philip used his head; Andrew used his eyes; the child used his heart. And Jesus chose the child's heart.
This reminds us: if we always look first at “not enough,” we stop the miracle; if we are willing to place “everything” in Jesus' hands, He begins to work.

This passage also makes us think: many times we feel our time is not enough, our ability too small, our resources limited, our circumstances hard, as if nothing is enough for God to use. But the Lord is not waiting for us to become more, stronger, or better; He is waiting for us to be “willing to hand it over to Him.”
Human hands calculate, but the Lord's hands multiply. Human eyes limit, but the Lord's eyes see possibility.
The five loaves and two fish in the child's hands were not enough; in Jesus' hands they were a breakthrough.

Everyone has five loaves and two fish in life. Yours may be your prayer, your time, your gifts, your small faith, your heart that longs to change. If you are willing to offer them as simply as a child, the Lord can do in your life more than you ask or think.
q: What “loaves and fish” in your life look “not enough”?
Today, are you willing to hand them to Jesus like a child?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, give us a simple heart, to look not at how many loaves there are but to learn to place what we have in Jesus' hands. Help us not to be limited by “not enough” or defeated by “too little,” but to believe that the Lord can use every bit of the heart we offer. Give us courage, so that like a child we give our lives entirely to You. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” Now there was much grass in that place. So the men sat down, in number about five thousand.
Jesus took the loaves; and having given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to those who were sitting down; likewise also of the fish as much as they desired.
When they were filled, he said to his disciples, “Gather up the broken pieces which are left over, that nothing be lost.”
b: This passage describes the process of the miracle of the five loaves and two fish, but the real focus is not the food but Jesus' heart—His order, His faith, His thanksgiving, His provision, His restraint. Every detail is teaching material for the disciples' lives.

First, Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” This sentence seems simple but is deeply spiritual. Five thousand hungry men, plus women and children, everyone eager to eat; the disciples too were anxious, not knowing what to do.
But the first thing Jesus did was not to distribute food, not to solve the problem, not to perform the miracle at once; He said, “Have the people sit down.”

It means: first be quiet, first be steady, first trust. Before a miracle, the Lord first prepares people's hearts. For panic cannot experience God, haste cannot understand the Lord, and only a heart that sits down can see what God does.

And the text says, “Now there was much grass in the place.” This is no accident. God had already prepared a grassy place for them to sit, so that the people might receive God's provision in rest. The Lord not only provides food but also rest; He not only feeds the body but also shepherds the soul.
Next, Jesus took the loaves and gave thanks. Notice: He did not take “enough” loaves; He gave thanks when there was “not enough”; He did not give thanks after being satisfied; He gave thanks in lack.
People give thanks when they see abundance; Jesus gave thanks when He saw the Father.

He knew that the loaves were not about size, provision not about quantity, abundance not about appearance, and power not in these five loaves and two fish themselves, but in the Father's faithfulness.

To give thanks is to turn our eyes from “my not enough” to “the Father's abundance.” To give thanks is to greet God's work with faith. To give thanks is to declare that the source of provision is not man but God.

Then Jesus began to distribute to those who were seated. In the Lord's hands the small loaves were given out again and again and again, until everyone received and everyone was filled. The text says, “as much as they desired.” Not grudging, not patched together, not given sparingly, but “given enough according to need.”
What people give is limited, what Jesus gives is sufficient, what the Father gives is abundant.
The five loaves and two fish in the disciples' hands were handed over to the Lord, and finally five thousand were filled. This was not “becoming more” but “being used by the Lord.”
If we are willing to hand over, the Lord is willing to multiply.
Finally, when all were filled, Jesus said, “Gather up the broken pieces which remain, that nothing be lost.”
This sentence is also extremely important. Jesus did not say, “Throw them away generously”; He said, “Gather them up.”
This shows us three things about the Lord:
First, abundance is not waste. God delights in abundance, but He does not permit waste.
Second, a miracle is not extravagance. The greater the miracle, the greater the reverence.
Third, every provision God gives has value. The Lord could do more miracles, yet He still treasures every crumb of bread and every scrap of fish.
What Jesus values is not an “inflated miracle” but “provision from the Father.” This is His heart, and it is the heart the disciples must learn.
This passage reminds us:
First, sit down first, be quiet, focus. The Lord often first orders our hearts, then accomplishes His work.
Second, thanksgiving does not begin when we have abundance but when we lack. Thanksgiving in lack is the deepest expression of faith.
Third, put the small thing in Jesus' hands, and He can accomplish beyond our possibilities. The problem is not that the resource is small but whether we are willing to hand it over.
Fourth, after experiencing a miracle, we still need to treasure, be faithful, and revere. The Lord will enrich, but He does not allow us to waste.
q: Are you willing to “sit down” before the problem is solved?
Today, are you willing to give thanks even in lack and offer your little to Jesus?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, teach us to sit down first and wait on You without hurry. Give us a thankful heart, looking not at our lack but at Your abundance. Help us, like that child, to place everything in the hands of the Lord Jesus, so that You may do wonderful things in our lives. Teach us also to treasure every grace of Yours and to respond to Your provision with reverence. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: So they gathered them up, and filled twelve baskets with broken pieces from the five barley loaves, which were left over by those who had eaten.
When therefore the people saw the sign which Jesus did, they said, “This is truly the prophet who comes into the world.”
Jesus therefore, perceiving that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself.
b: This passage is the close of the miracle of the five loaves and two fish, but the real focus is not the satisfied crowd but Jesus' response. When people see a miracle, they easily exalt power; after performing the miracle, Jesus once again returned to the Father. This is a very important spiritual lesson in the disciples' lives: power is not the goal; obedience and focus are.

First, the disciples gathered up the broken pieces and filled twelve baskets. It was not “just twelve baskets left over” but “Jesus had them gather twelve baskets.” In the Bible, twelve symbolizes completeness, order, and divine authority. The purpose of the miracle was not to show off but to teach the disciples:

God's abundance is not waste, and the work of God has order. Each disciple carrying a basket was the Lord's own testimony to them: “See how I multiplied what you handed over; see that I do not perform miracles only for the crowd, I am also building you.”
These twelve baskets are not merely a number but a reminder: what you offer in God's hands will never be in vain; He will let you carry grace home with your own hands.

Then, when the people saw the miracle, they said, “This is truly the prophet who is coming into the world!” They did see what God did, but they misread God's heart. They thought Jesus was a king come to solve livelihood problems, a leader come to overthrow the regime, a king come to feed, heal, and give benefits.
What they saw was a miracle, but Jesus' heart was on the cross. What they saw was an earthly king, but Jesus' mission was the kingdom of heaven.
What they saw was being filled, but what Jesus wanted to give was eternal life.
People often take a miracle as the goal, but a miracle is only a signpost pointing to Jesus. People want Jesus to meet their needs, but Jesus' aim is to save their lives.
So verse 15 says, “Jesus therefore perceiving that they were about to come and take him by force, to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself alone.”
This sentence is the most startling part of the whole passage.
It is not that He could not be king; He is Lord of heaven and earth, and all things were made through Him.

But He refused to be the king “people thought” and was willing to be only the King “the Father sent.” He did not come to hold power; He came to fulfill His mission. He did not come for the crowd's cheers; He came for the cross.
After performing the miracle, Jesus did not stay on the stage; He went back to the mountain, to the place of being alone in fellowship with the Father.
This is the secret of His life: He was not drawn by human applause or bound by human expectations; He let only the Father's will guide all He did.
The miracle did not make Him proud, the need did not make Him flustered, the applause did not make Him deviate, the pressure did not make Him compromise.
His focus was always the Father, and His road was always the cross.
This passage reminds us:
First, God's provision always exceeds human need. The twelve baskets are the Lord's gentle encouragement to the disciples—He not only satisfies the crowd but also feeds those who follow Him.
Second, seeing a miracle is not the same as understanding God's heart. People often look at outward grace but do not understand the Lord's mission.

Third, do not let success scatter your focus. After the miracle Jesus did not stand at the front; He withdrew to the mountain. This is a lesson every servant must learn—after power, return to the Father; after grace, give the glory to God.
Fourth, do not let people's expectations become our direction. The crowd wanted to make Him king, but Jesus went up the mountain to seek the Father's will. He was not pleasing people but obeying God.
q: After experiencing grace or success, are you drawn by applause, or are you willing, like Jesus, to return to “the mountain” to be with the Father?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, teach us to be like Jesus, not drawn by people's applause or bound by people's expectations, simply seeking Your will. Teach us to see grace as Your blessing and not our merit; to treat success as a moment to return to You and not a reason to leave You. After every experience of abundance, make us long more to align with You and walk more steadfastly in Your will. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea.
They entered into the boat, and were going over the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not come to them.
The sea was tossed by a great wind blowing.
b: On the surface these three verses are scenery description, but they are in fact the spiritual condition every disciple's life will pass through: darkness, no direction, the Lord not in sight, a storm suddenly arriving. This is no accident but a training Jesus deliberately designed—He had just refused the people who wanted to force Him to be king, and now He lets the disciples face another deep lesson: when they cannot see Him, will they still believe Him?

First, the text says, “When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea.” In the daytime they had just experienced the stunning miracle of the five loaves and two fish, the people filled, the disciples' baskets full, grace overflowing. But spiritual life is never standing on the mountaintop all the time; often just after grace, training comes.
God often leads us into training after a blessing; for a miracle excites people, but only the storm shapes them.
Next, verse 17 says, “It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.” This sentence is deeply meaningful.
Dark—the outside circumstances are blurred; Jesus had not come—inwardly they could not sense the Lord's presence.

Most people can trust in the light, but when it is dark, can you still believe? It is easy to believe when we can see; true faith is when we cannot. Jesus did not at once go forward in the boat with them; He let the disciples experience—faith is built not on feeling but on trust in the Lord.
The disciples knew Jesus had told them to go ahead, but when the surroundings darkened and the sea wind rose, their hearts naturally wavered. This also reflects our lives:

Sometimes it is clearly the road the Lord told us to walk, and yet as we go it suddenly feels dark, tiring, and as if He has not come. But the Lord's delay is not forgetfulness; He is preparing a deeper meeting with us.
Then the text says, “A great wind blew.” Life's storms are often like this—sudden. Problems come suddenly, pressure comes suddenly, attacks come suddenly, fear comes suddenly.

This was not the first time the disciples had met a storm at sea, but “Jesus not being in the boat” gave this storm a completely different weight. They were not afraid of the wind but afraid of being without the Lord. The waves were not the main problem; faith was the main problem.
Jesus let the storm come, not to destroy the disciples but to make them understand: when He is not before their eyes, He still reigns; when He is not in the boat, He still watches over them.

Everyone who loves the Lord has this experience in life: it gets dark—we cannot see the road; the Lord has not yet come—we feel He is far; the wind rises—trouble presses in; the sea churns—the heart begins to panic.
But this is not the Lord's absence; this is the Lord preparing to enter.
He is not failing to come; He is waiting for the best moment, so that the disciples may see He is not only the Lord who fed five thousand but also the Lord who rules the wind and waves.
This passage reminds us:
First, God often gives us training after grace. A miracle builds the spark of faith; the storm builds its foundation.
Second, not seeing Jesus does not mean He is not there. His silence is not forgetting but shaping.
Third, the hour of darkness is the real examination room of faith. Anyone can believe in the light; only those who still believe in the dark truly know Him.
Fourth, a storm is often the announcement that the Lord is about to appear. The darker the night, the nearer the dawn.
q: Are you facing a season in your life of “dark, the Lord not yet come, and the wind rising again”?
In such a moment, are you willing to choose to believe that He is coming toward you?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, when we meet darkness, storm, and delay, let us not doubt or panic but firmly believe that You still reign. Increase our faith in every trial, so that we rely neither on sight nor on feeling but know that You are coming toward us. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: When therefore they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia,  they saw Jesus walking on the sea, and drawing near to the boat; and they were afraid.
But he said to them, “It is I. Don’t be afraid.”
They were willing therefore to receive him into the boat. Immediately the boat was at the land where they were going.
b: This passage is the peak of the storm, the Lord's gentlest and most authoritative self-revelation. The disciples were caught in darkness, waves, weariness, and fear, and at that very moment Jesus came toward them in a way they had never seen. This was no ordinary help; it showed that He is the Lord who transcends nature, transcends hardship, and rules the wind and the sea.

The text says, “When therefore they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia.” They had labored a long time, hard, strained, breathless. But the harder they tried, the greater the waves and the slower their progress. Even seasoned fishermen were helpless. This picture is a spiritual symbol:
Some storms cannot be weathered by effort; some roads cannot be rowed by ability; some hardships are overcome not by strength but by Jesus.
People grow tired, strength runs out, methods fail, but Jesus is never late.
Just when the disciples were weakest and most helpless, “they saw Jesus walking on the sea, and drawing near to the boat.”
Notice these three levels:
First, “saw Jesus”—revelation; second, “walking on the sea”—the Lord's authority; third, “drawing near”—the Lord comes close to you

Jesus did not stand on the shore and shout; He walked on the waves the disciples feared most toward them. He used what they thought most dangerous as the road beneath His feet. He let them know: the waves you fear are the road under My feet; the circumstances you see as a threat are the stage on which I display My authority.
But how did the disciples react? “They were afraid.”
They were not afraid of the storm; they were afraid of Jesus!
Why? Because they could not see Him clearly, because He came to them in a way they had never seen, because His work went beyond their understanding.

We are often the same: when God steps into our lives in ways unfamiliar, unaccustomed, or unexpected, we become afraid instead of believing. God's work is often greater than we imagine, His methods more wonderful, and His timing less predictable.
Just as the disciples were afraid, Jesus spoke the warmest words in the New Testament:
“It is I. Don't be afraid.”

These words came earlier than the calming of the storm and mattered more than the calm sea. For beyond the wind and waves, what the disciples truly needed was: in the midst of chaos, to be sure that Jesus is there.
“It is I”—His presence; “Don't be afraid”—His comfort and authority

This is what Jesus says to every child in a storm. He did not say, “The waves are not big,” or “Be strong,” or “Hold on.” He said, “It is I.” He turned their attention from the storm back to Himself. For the first step is not the solution but focus.
Then the text says, “They were willing therefore to receive him into the boat.”
A moment ago afraid, now full of joy. True peace is not a calm sea but Jesus in the boat.
As soon as the Lord was in the boat, “immediately the boat was at the land where they were going.”
This is the most wonderful sentence. The disciples had rowed twenty-five or thirty stadia and were still in the storm; once Jesus got in, they arrived at the destination at once.
This represents three spiritual truths:

First, effort without Jesus is toilsome, with results but without effect; second, Jesus' leading is swift, accurate, and full of grace; third, what matters most in life is not speed but who is in the boat.

You can row very fast in the wrong direction; you can row very hard and be blocked by wind and waves; but as long as Jesus is in the boat, He can accomplish in a moment what you could not in years of effort.
This passage reminds us:
First, the storm is not the real problem; not recognizing Jesus is. He often comes to you in ways you never expected.
Second, true peace is not a change of circumstances but the Lord saying, “It is I, don't be afraid.” His voice is greater than the waves.
Third, receiving Jesus into the boat is receiving Him into the very center of life. He is not only a helper; He is Lord.
Fourth, with Him present, life will travel the road He has prepared, accurately and without delay. He can bring you in an instant to the place He wants you to be.
q: Are you now rowing hard in your own strength?
Are you willing to stop being afraid, joyfully invite Jesus into the boat, and let Him take you to the place He has prepared for you?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for letting us know that in storm, darkness, and weariness, Jesus is coming toward us. Teach us to hear His voice, recognize His presence, and joyfully receive Him into the boat of our lives. May we no longer row in our own strength but move forward by Your guidance. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: On the next day, the multitude that stood on the other side of the sea saw that there was no other boat there, except the one in which his disciples had embarked, and that Jesus hadn’t entered with his disciples into the boat, but his disciples had gone away alone.
However boats from Tiberias came near to the place where they ate the bread after the Lord had given thanks.
