He did not “say whatever He wanted to say”; every word He spoke was in complete agreement with the Father. His teaching was not a human theory but God's revelation. His words were not learned but came from heaven.
He was not passing on knowledge; He was revealing God's heart.
Finally, Jesus said something extremely key, extremely upside-down, and extremely true:
“If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God, or if I speak from myself.”
In this sentence Jesus uncovers the core principle of spiritual understanding:
The key to understanding truth is not the head but the heart. Not cleverness but obedience. Not understanding first and then acting, but being willing to act first, and then understanding.
The world's way is: understand → accept → act.
Jesus' way is: surrender → act → see → understand.

If a person is unwilling to surrender, even a lifetime of study will not let him truly understand truth. But a person willing to obey God's will, even if he does not understand at first, will be guided, revealed to, and made to see by God Himself.
True spiritual light does not come from research but from obedience.
This passage reminds us:
First, Jesus never acted on man's timetable but on the Father's time. In the Father's timing, He speaks naturally, teaches naturally, and fulfills His mission naturally.
Second, spiritual authority does not come from human education but from God's calling. Jesus had not been trained in the religious system, yet He possessed wisdom from heaven.
Third, if people judge only with the mind, they easily become proud like the Jews, measuring God by human ways.
Fourth, true revelation comes from obedience. “If anyone desires to do God's will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God.”
Fifth, faith is not understanding first and then doing, but being willing first to surrender and to believe, and then God makes us understand.
q: In seeking truth now, do you depend on understanding or on obedience?
Are you willing to say to the Lord, “I am willing to do Your will; please help me understand Your word”?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, give us a teachable heart, so that we no longer measure Your truth by human methods. Make us willing to obey first and understand afterward; to believe first and see afterward. Lead us into Your light, so that we truly know that the teaching of Jesus comes from You and is life, the way, and the truth. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory, but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and no unrighteousness is in him.
Didn’t Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keeps the law? Why do you seek to kill me?”
The multitude answered, “You have a demon! Who seeks to kill you?”
b: This passage is Jesus' response to the Jews' questioning of His teaching. He brings out two things: (1) the motive behind speaking; (2) the gap between religious appearance and real life. His answer does not only respond to the question; it also shines light into the heart.
Jesus first says:
“He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory.”
He points out a spiritual principle: the source of a person's speech determines the nature of his speech.
If a person speaks from himself—in order to be seen, affirmed, respected, exalted—then however spiritual his words, they will carry unrighteousness.
A person may not look proud on the outside, but as long as the heart is seeking its own glory, the words that come out will deviate from the truth.
Then He adds the contrast:
“But he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and no unrighteousness is in him.”
It means: a true servant does not want people to notice himself but to notice God. Not to highlight himself but to let the glory go to the Heavenly Father who sent him.
Jesus never sought His own glory in His whole life. All His words, all His decisions, all His actions had only one motive: that the Heavenly Father be glorified.
This is why He is true, upright, and pure. There is not a trace of unrighteousness in Him, because there is not a trace of self.
He is saying: if a person seeks God's glory, his life is true; if a person seeks his own glory, his life will be twisted by unrighteousness.
Then in verse 19 He points out the deepest problem:
“Didn't Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keeps the law? Why do you seek to kill me?”
Jesus lays bare the hypocrisy of religion:
With your mouths you honor Moses, honor the law, and say you love God, but your actions violate the most basic requirement of the law: do not murder.
What He means is: the law you value most, you yourselves do not keep. Outwardly you are spiritual, but inwardly you resist the truth.
However beautiful the religious exterior, if life is not surrendered it falls into falsehood.
As soon as Jesus said this, the people's hearts were lit up, but they were unwilling to admit the truth about themselves.
So verse 20 contains an extremely ironic line:
“You have a demon! Who seeks to kill you?”
When truth shines on people, if they are unwilling to be illumined, they attack the light, deny the light, accuse the light.
When they said Jesus “has a demon,” they were really saying: “It is not that something is wrong with us; something is wrong with you!”
But as the Gospel goes on, the people's intent to kill Jesus becomes clearer and clearer, and in the end they really did nail Him to the cross.
Those unwilling to face the truth will attack the one who points it out.
This passage reminds us:
First, the motive of speaking determines the spiritual quality of speaking. If it is for ourselves, words easily deviate from truth; if it is for God, words can bring forth life.
Second, those truly of God do not seek their own glory but seek God's will. A surrendered person has no unrighteousness in his heart.
Third, a religious exterior without life easily leads to self-deception. The Jews honored the law yet broke the law; we too may honor God's word without truly doing it.
Fourth, when truth shines into the heart, people respond in one of two ways: (1) humble surrender; (2) counterattack and denial. The more unwilling a person is to surrender, the greater his attack.
Fifth, the power of Jesus' life is that He was completely emptied of self—He did not speak His own words, did not seek His own glory, did not do His own will.
q: Are your motives in speaking and serving truly for God, or for yourself?
Today, are you willing to ask the Lord to make you a person in whom “no unrighteousness is found”?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, make our hearts pure, so that everything we say and do is for Your glory and not our own. Shine on us, so that we do not fall into the trap of religious appearance but truly do Your will. When truth shines on us, give us humility, so that we do not counterattack or hide but surrender in You. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Jesus answered them, “I did one work and you all marvel because of it.
Moses has given you circumcision (not that it is of Moses, but of the fathers), and on the Sabbath you circumcise a boy.
If a boy receives circumcision on the Sabbath, that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me, because I made a man completely healthy on the Sabbath?
Don’t judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment.”
b: In this passage the theme Jesus brings out is: human eyes are often distorted, but God's eyes are always righteous. True spiritual life is to let go of judging by appearance and enter into judging by God's heart.
At the beginning, Jesus says:
“I did one work, and you all marvel because of it.”

This “one work” was the healing of the paralyzed man by the pool of Bethesda on the Sabbath (John 5). Jesus had not done many perplexing things; He had done only one—healing a man who had suffered for many years.

But the religious people accused Him and opposed Him because of the “Sabbath.” They did not see God's merciful heart, only the rules they kept; they did not see the grace of healing, only outward conduct.
This reflects a common problem of religious people: they value form over life; letter over mercy; rules over God Himself. Jesus knew this well and confronted it directly.
So He continues:
“Moses has given you circumcision (not that it is of Moses, but of the fathers), and on the Sabbath you circumcise a boy.”

Jesus points out a contradiction: in order to keep circumcision, the Jews would circumcise a baby even on the Sabbath. Why? Because circumcision is the sign of the covenant with God, and they dared not delay. In other words, they themselves made “exceptions” on the Sabbath.

Yet when Jesus healed a man who had suffered for many years, they were furious. This shows that their problem was not the law but the heart. The law was meant to bring life to people, not to make them lose life. But they turned the law into a burden, an accusation, a bondage.
Then Jesus asks:
“If a boy receives circumcision on the Sabbath, that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me, because I made a man every bit whole on the Sabbath?”

What He means is: you can act on the Sabbath in order to keep circumcision; but I may not act in order to restore a person's life? What you keep is the form; what I keep is the essence of life. You value rules; I value the Father's heart.
Jesus is saying: true rest is not doing nothing but being in agreement with the Father's heart; true obedience is not clinging to the letter but living out God's love.
Finally, Jesus speaks the most important sentence of this passage:
“Don't judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment.”
Judging by appearance is human nature: looking at the exterior, the ritual, the habit, the culture, other people's behavior, the way we like.
But God looks at the heart, at motives, at essence, at life. He does not judge by appearance but by truth.
“Judge righteous judgment” in the original means: “by God's standard, not man's standard.” That is—turn your eyes from earthly eyes to God's eyes; not looking at the surface but at God's heart.
This passage reminds us:
First, the religious eye easily sees rules but not life. Jesus healed a person, yet they looked only at whether the Sabbath was being “violated.”
Second, people often judge by appearance rather than by God's heart. Appearance easily deceives, and easily makes people think themselves righteous.
Third, everything Jesus did was in accord with the Father's heart. He was not destroying the Sabbath; He was restoring the true meaning of the Sabbath.
Fourth, what God values is not ritual but life. He cares more about people being healed and set free than about rigid religious appearance.
Fifth, truly spiritual people do not “look at appearance” but “judge righteous judgment”—by God's eyes, by God's truth, by God's heart.
q: Have you also ever overlooked God's true heart because of appearance, form, or human habit?
Today, are you willing to ask the Lord to give you His eyes, to see the essence of things and His will?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, remove our habit of looking at appearances, so that we no longer judge things by human standards but see everything with Your eyes. Bring our hearts back to the essence of life, not stuck in dead rules but living in Your truth and love. Help us, like Jesus, to do everything in a way that reflects Your heart. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Therefore some of them of Jerusalem said, “Isn’t this he whom they seek to kill?
Behold, he speaks openly, and they say nothing to him. Can it be that the rulers indeed know that this is truly the Christ?
However we know where this man comes from, but when the Christ comes, no one will know where he comes from.”
b: This passage shows us three reactions of the human heart: the confused, the watchful, and the rejecting. In Jesus' public teaching, each reaction reveals the heart's attitude toward truth, and also shows how people, because of their own notions, miss the moment when God Himself comes to them.
The passage first says:
“Isn't this he whom they seek to kill?”

Among the people in Jerusalem, some had already sensed the intentions of the religious leaders and had heard that Jesus was being hunted. They knew the authorities wanted to kill Jesus and understood the political and religious opposition behind it. Yet now they saw—Jesus standing in front of everyone speaking openly, and those who wanted to kill Him did nothing to stop Him.

This puzzled them greatly. One of the greatest obstacles of the human heart to faith is “confusion” and “contradiction.” On one hand they had heard the rulers wanted to kill Him; on the other they saw the rulers doing nothing. So they began to reason, doubt, and guess.
Then they said:
“Can it be that the rulers indeed know that this is truly the Christ?”

These words reveal the wavering in their hearts: the rulers had said He was a heretic and a false prophet, but now they let Him teach publicly—could it mean the rulers were beginning to believe in Him?
Their faith was not rooted in God but in the leaders' attitude; not rooted in truth but in the voice of social mainstream.
This also exposes a common phenomenon: some people are not seeking truth but watching power and the direction of the wind.
If the rulers believe, they are willing to believe; if the rulers oppose, they follow in opposing. This is not faith but group psychology.
Verse 27 shows another, deeper problem:
“However we know where this man comes from, but when the Christ comes, no one will know where he comes from.”
They thought they “knew” Jesus' background, so they concluded He could not be the Christ. Their logic was:
“We know where Jesus is from—Nazareth. But the Christ should be mysteriously sent by God, and no one should know His origin.”
They had a set of imaginings about “what the Messiah should be like,” but these imaginings did not come from Scripture at all; they came from human tradition, human expectation, and human memory.

They took their own notions as truth, and so: the truth was in front of them, yet they could not see it. The Savior was before their eyes, yet they did not recognize Him. Christ stood among them in person, yet they rejected Him because of their notions.
Once a person places his own thinking above God's revelation, he falls from “thinking he knows” to “missing it completely.”
This passage gives us important reminders:

First, some people cannot believe because of confusion and contradiction. They look at people, circumstances, and the direction of the wind, but do not sincerely look at Jesus. Faith not built on Jesus is shaky faith.
Second, some follow power rather than truth. They watch the rulers' attitude more than God's will. Such faith will keep wavering with outside changes.
Third, some reject Jesus because of their own notions. They think they have grasped the truth, yet what they think is right blocks God's true revelation.
Fourth, the greatest blindness is not “not knowing” but “thinking we know.” This makes it harder to surrender, harder to turn, harder to believe.
Fifth, Jesus is right before their eyes, but the truth about the human heart is revealed in how it reacts to Him—the humble see Him, the proud miss Him.
q: With what eyes do you look at Jesus today?
Do you follow human thinking, or are you willing to lay down your own notions and receive the truth He reveals to you Himself?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, remove every blindness from our hearts, so that we no longer limit Your work with our own notions. Let us no longer look at people's opinions, no longer watch the wind, no longer follow the mainstream, but look to You alone. Give us humble hearts, willing to admit that Your thoughts are higher than our thoughts and Your ways higher than our ways. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Jesus therefore cried out in the temple, teaching and saying, “You both know me, and know where I am from. I have not come of myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you don’t know.
I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me.”
They sought therefore to take him; but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come.
But of the multitude, many believed in him. They said, “When the Christ comes, he won’t do more signs than those which this man has done, will he?”
b: This passage unfolds a vivid contrast: the clearer the truth, the more hearts are divided. The brighter the light shines, the stronger people react.
The passage begins:
“Jesus therefore cried out in the temple, teaching and saying, ‘You both know me, and know where I am from…’”

Jesus was not weak or afraid to state His identity openly; He was not discussing it in secret but proclaiming it loudly. He did not fear the threats of the religious leaders; He was faithful to the truth and to His mission.
He said:
“I have not come of myself.”
Once more He declares that His origin is not earthly, that He is not here for Himself, not for fame, position, or applause; everything He does is because the Father sent Him.
His life is completely emptied of self, His actions come entirely from the Father's will, and His words are in complete accord with the Father's heart.
Then He says:
“He who sent me is true, whom you don't know.”
Here Jesus points out their spiritual blind spot: they thought they knew God, thought they were familiar with the law, the temple, and the tradition, but they did not actually know the true God.
They looked at the temple but did not know God's heart; they carried the law but did not understand the Lord of the law; they saw Jesus but could not see the Father.
Religion can make people “think they know God,” but only Jesus can make people truly know God.
Jesus continues:
“I know him, because I am from him, and he sent me.”

He does not know God vaguely but completely; He does not understand God from afar but is wholly one with the Father. He knows the Father's heart, the Father's will, the Father's plan. He is from the Father and also in the Father.
The reason His words carry authority and power is precisely that He has an incomparably intimate relationship with the Father at the root.
Next the passage describes a strong reaction:
“They sought therefore to take him.”

Why? Because His words exposed their true spiritual condition: they thought they belonged to God but did not actually know God. When the light shone into the depths of their hearts, they were unwilling to repent and instead wanted to get rid of the one who lit them up.
Yet:
“No one laid his hand on him, because his hour had not yet come.”

No one can move earlier than God, no plan can outrun God's timing, no attack can break through God's protection. Jesus' life was completely within the Father's time, and no one could send Him to the cross ahead of schedule.
Whoever is in God's hand, no darkness can take his life; only when God's time comes will things be accomplished.
Finally, the passage ends with a beautiful picture:
“But of the multitude, many believed in him.”
Although some hated Him, rejected Him, and opposed Him, there were also those who believed in Him because of His miracles, His words, and His life.
They said:
“When the Christ comes, will he do more signs than those which this man has done?”

This is a sober recognition: if Jesus is not the Christ, who else could be? The signs He did, His teaching, the love He showed, all made clear that He was no ordinary man. Their hearts were illumined, and they were willing to receive the light.
This passage reminds us:
First, Jesus always speaks according to truth, not according to people's emotions or circumstances. He proclaims the Father's will loudly, without compromise.
Second, if people stay at the religious exterior, they will “think they know God” without truly knowing Him. The One who truly knows God is Jesus, and He leads us into true knowledge.
Third, when truth is spoken plainly, people show the real state of their lives. Some oppose, some believe; truth always divides people.
Fourth, even when people attack and try to seize Jesus, they cannot do so ahead of God's time. Those who walk in God's will are safe and secure.
Fifth, true faith begins with seeing what Jesus says and does. Those who seek will see, the humble will hear, and the willing will believe.
q: Is your knowledge of Jesus today still in your head, or has it gone deep into your heart?
Are you willing to let His great light shine on you, so that you come to know the Father's heart more?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, open our hearts completely to You, so that we do not stay at religious surface but truly know You. Help us not to reject the light and not to fear the truth, but to be willing to be illumined, guided, and changed. Let our lives be completely in Your timing, because we know that You are in control of all things. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: The Pharisees heard the multitude murmuring these things concerning him, and the chief priests and the Pharisees sent officers to arrest him.
Then Jesus said, “I will be with you a little while longer, then I go to him who sent me.
You will seek me, and won’t find me. You can’t come where I am.”
The Jews therefore said among themselves, “Where will this man go that we won’t find him? Will he go to the Dispersion among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks?
What is this word that he said, ‘You will seek me, and won’t find me;’ and ‘Where I am, you can’t come’?”
b: This passage uncovers a profound truth: people reject Jesus because they do not know Him; people may seek Jesus yet never find Him again. The key is not that Jesus hides but that the human heart is closed.
The passage begins:
“The Pharisees heard the multitude murmuring these things concerning him, and the chief priests and the Pharisees sent officers to arrest him.”

The reason they wanted to arrest Jesus was not that He had done anything wrong, but that His truth shook their position, system, and control. When the heart is controlled by power, the clearer the truth, the more hostile they become.
The Pharisees' reaction tells us: some people do not fail to know the truth; they are unwilling to have it. They do not lack light; they are unwilling to let the light in.
Jesus saw their hearts and knew the time the Father had arranged, so He declared:
“I will be with you a little while longer, then I go to him who sent me.”
Jesus' life was not taken from Him; He completed His mission in the time the Father had set. He knew His time on earth was short and fixed, that no one could shorten it and no one could lengthen it.

He was not running away from people but moving toward the goal the Father had set. He was saying: “My time with you is limited. You can hear Me, see Me, touch Me, respond to Me—but such moments will not last forever.”
Then He says:
“You will seek me, and won't find me; and where I am, you can't come.”
This sentence is deeply startling:
If a person rejects Jesus in the days of opportunity, there will come a day when, even if he wants to find Him, he cannot.
It is not that Jesus is unwilling to be found, but that people have refused for so long that their hearts have turned to stone.
“You can't come” is not because the distance is too great, but because the heart is too hard, too proud, too unwilling to repent, and so has lost the ability to enter His presence.
Jesus was foretelling that He would return to the Father, but none of those who rejected Him could get there by themselves.
Because the only way to the Father is He Himself. To reject Him is to reject the way itself.
Then the Jews' reaction reveals their blindness:
“Where will this man go that we won't find him? Will he go to the Dispersion among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks?”
They explained everything with earthly eyes and guessed with human logic. They thought Jesus was talking about geography, not knowing He was speaking of heavenly truth.

This is the greatest predicament of those who do not know Jesus: they hear His words and do not understand; they see His actions and do not comprehend; He speaks of heavenly things, and people explain them with earthly notions.
Finally, the passage says:
“What is this word that he said?”

They did not understand because they refused to let truth shine into their hearts. Without repentance, they cannot hear. Without surrender, they cannot see. Without willingness to believe, they cannot enter His revelation.
This passage reminds us:
First, some people care not about truth but about maintaining their position. The more such people hear the truth, the more they want to seize Jesus.
Second, Jesus' presence with people is grace, not something to take for granted. He gives everyone time to repent and believe, but that time is not forever.
Third, those who reject Jesus will one day seek Him and not find Him. It is not that Jesus hides, but that the heart can no longer respond.
Fourth, looking at heavenly things with earthly eyes leads to complete error. Heavenly things require humility, surrender, and the illumination of the Holy Spirit.
Fifth, the only ones who can truly reach the Father are those who are willing to receive Jesus. He is the way, the truth, and the life; unless through Him, no one can come to the Father.
q: Are you experiencing Jesus' reminder, call, and invitation today?
Are you willing, while He can still be found, to respond to Him and surrender to Him with all your heart?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, soften our hearts, so that we not only hear Your word but are willing to respond to Your call. Let us not miss the moment You have given us, not harden our hearts or close the door of our hearts. Help us understand that those who can truly reach You are those who humbly receive Jesus and surrender in His grace. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Now on the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink!
He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.”
But he said this about the Spirit, which those believing in him were to receive. For the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus wasn’t yet glorified.
b: These three verses are the climax of the whole chapter, Jesus' mightiest declaration at the Feast of Tabernacles. Before the crowd He unveils a stunning truth: He did not come to give people religion, but life; not rituals, but living water; not doctrines, but the Holy Spirit.
The passage begins:
“Now on the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out…”

The last day of the Feast of Tabernacles was the day of greatest joy. The priests would draw water and pour it out, symbolizing a prayer that God would send rain, and pointing ahead to the hope that God would give the fountain of life.

At this very moment, when water was being so deliberately emphasized, Jesus stood up and cried out: the true water, the true life, the true fountain is not a ritual, not a water jar, not a religious tradition, but Himself.
In that moment He fulfilled the symbolism of the entire feast.
He said:
“If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink!”
He did not speak only to one group. Not to the meritorious, not to those who knew the law, not to the religious elite. He spoke to “anyone” who is thirsty.
Only the thirsty can drink. Only those who know their lack can receive. Only those who admit they cannot can obtain.
He does not give to the satisfied but to the thirsty; not to the self-righteous but to those who know they are not able.
And what He gives is not a temporary supply, not a cup of water, but eternal living water.
Then He said:
“He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.”
He does not only want to quench our thirst; He wants to make us a fountain.
He does not want us to be only receivers; He wants us to be channels.
Living water does not stay inside; it flows out. Life is not only for ourselves; it overflows to others. The Holy Spirit does not only give grace; He makes grace a river of life.
Here are three important revelations:
First, “from within him” means the deepest place, the human spirit. God's life does not stay on the surface; it enters the innermost being.
Second, “living water” is not stagnant water, not religion, not knowledge; it is the Holy Spirit, who is able to change a life.
Third, “rivers” are not a trickle, not an occasional drip, but a continuous, surging, overflowing life.
This is not something people produce; it is something the Holy Spirit causes to flow out.
Verse 39 reveals the heart of it all:
“But he said this about the Spirit, which those believing in him were to receive.”

Jesus was not talking about devotional techniques, inner healing, or religious feelings. He was declaring that true life comes from the Holy Spirit, the true fountain is the Holy Spirit, true satisfaction is the Holy Spirit, and true power is the Holy Spirit.
Without the Holy Spirit, people only thirst. With the Holy Spirit, people are not only satisfied, but through us others can be satisfied too.
The text adds:
“For the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus wasn’t yet glorified.”
What is Jesus' glory? The cross, the resurrection, the ascension. After Jesus was glorified, He poured out the Holy Spirit so that everyone who believes in Him would become a channel of living water.
This passage reminds us:
First, Jesus did not come to establish a religion but to give life. His goal is not that we keep rules, but that we receive living water.
Second, only the thirsty come to Jesus. Those who think they are satisfied will not come before Him.
Third, coming to Him is not a work but a relationship; not effort but belief; not performance but surrender.
Fourth, true life is not receiving a little but flowing without end. The Holy Spirit is not a passing inspiration but a continuous fountain.
Fifth, Jesus wants us not only to be filled but to overflow. He does not want us to be a water jar, but a river.
q: Is your life dry today, or flowing?
Are you willing to give your heart completely to the Holy Spirit and let Him make you rivers of living water?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, we admit that we are often thirsty inside. The water of the world cannot satisfy us; only the living water of Jesus can truly give us life. Today we come before You. May Your Holy Spirit fill us, so that we are not only satisfied but become channels of living water, letting life flow out from within us. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Many of the multitude therefore, when they heard these words, said, “This is truly the prophet.”
Others said, “This is the Christ.” But some said, “What, does the Christ come out of Galilee?
Hasn’t the Scripture said that the Christ comes of the offspring of David,  and from Bethlehem, the village where David was?”
So a division arose in the multitude because of him.
Some of them would have arrested him, but no one laid hands on him.
b: This passage shows how Jesus' words and His presence immediately expose the human heart. The same Jesus, the same teaching, the same scene, yet completely different reactions: some believe, some misunderstand, some reject, some become hostile. Truth does not make everyone agree; it makes everyone take a stand.
The passage begins:
“Many of the multitude therefore, when they heard these words, said, ‘This is truly the prophet.’”

“The prophet” refers to the prophet Moses foretold in Deuteronomy 18, the coming Messianic leader like Moses. These people saw Jesus' authority, His life, and His teaching full of grace and truth, and in their hearts they recognized that He was no ordinary rabbi; He was the one God had promised.
But they did not yet understand enough. They acknowledged Him only as “the prophet,” not as “the Christ.” Their eyes had begun to be enlightened, but they did not yet see clearly.
Then another group went further:
“Others said, ‘This is the Christ.’”
These people saw Jesus' miracles, His love, His authority, and His life, and in their hearts they were sure: this is not an ordinary man, not just a prophet, but the Christ sent from God.
True faith in a crowd is often small and not the mainstream, but it is always there. Jesus' light lets those who humbly seek God see the truth.
Yet there are always those who oppose.
Verses 41 and 42 show a third reaction:
“But some said, ‘What, does the Christ come out of Galilee?’” “Hasn’t the Scripture said that the Christ comes of the offspring of David, and from Bethlehem?”
Their objection was not based on truth but on mistaken information they thought they “knew.”
They thought Jesus was a Galilean, not knowing He was actually born in Bethlehem. They thought He was not a descendant of David, not knowing He was exactly that.
Their objection came not from the truth but from ignorance, prejudice, hearsay, and wrong impressions.

This is a deep reminder to us: the human heart most easily rejects God's fullest revelation because of incomplete information. A wrong understanding of Jesus is more deadly than not knowing Him at all.
Their wrong ideas raised a wall that kept them from seeing the true Christ.
Then the text says:
“So a division arose in the multitude because of him.”
Such an outcome is not an accident but a certainty.

When truth appears, the crowd is bound to be divided. The brighter the light, the more the heart is revealed. Jesus does not let people stay neutral; He wants them to declare their position rather than drift vaguely along with the crowd.
He did not come into the world to create confusion but to reveal what is real.
And the last verse shows a fourth reaction:
“Some of them would have arrested him, but no one laid hands on him.”
Toward Jesus' light they felt not gratitude but hatred. Not only did they not believe, they wanted to get rid of Him. But no one laid hands on Him, because:
One, Jesus' hour had not yet come;
Two, God's hand restrained them;
Three, Jesus' life was under the Father's protection;
Four, human malice cannot overcome God's purpose.
This passage reminds us:
First, those who hear the truth do not all react the same way. Some are drawn, some are enlightened, some are offended, and some become hostile.
Second, those who think they already know are the most likely to miss Christ. Those who thought Jesus came from Galilee were blocked by their own notions from knowing the Savior.
Third, if people rely only on surface information, they cannot know Jesus. We must seek humbly in order to see the truth.
Fourth, Jesus' coming completely exposes people's true spiritual condition. He is the light that discerns the heart.
Fifth, no attack could reach Jesus ahead of God's timing. In the same way, all who are in God's will are secure.
q: Do you know Jesus by your own ideas, or do you truly let Him reveal Himself to you?
Today, will you ask the Lord to enlighten your eyes so that you see that He truly is the Christ?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, we ask You to enlighten our eyes with Your true light, so that we no longer go by impressions or rely on human hearsay, but truly know Jesus by the Scriptures and the light of the Holy Spirit. Guard our hearts so that we do not fall into wrong notions, but receive only Your revelation. May we always stand on the side of truth and be willing to follow Christ to the end. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: The officers therefore came to the chief priests and Pharisees, and they said to them, “Why didn’t you bring him?”
The officers answered, “No man ever spoke like this man!”
The Pharisees therefore answered them, “You aren’t also led astray, are you?
Have any of the rulers believed in him, or of the Pharisees?
But this multitude that doesn’t know the law is cursed.”
b: This passage is a sharp contrast: on one side, officers shaken by Jesus' words; on the other, religious leaders bound by pride and power. All of them heard Jesus speak, yet some hearts were opened and some grew harder.
The passage begins:
“The officers therefore came to the chief priests and Pharisees.”
These officers had been sent to do one thing: arrest Jesus. They went with orders, but came back empty-handed.
The religious leaders were displeased and immediately demanded:
“Why didn’t you bring him?”
In their eyes, Jesus was only a “target,” a “problem,” a “threat.” They did not care about truth, only about control. What they expected was obedience to orders, not hearing the truth.
But the officers' answer was striking:
“No man ever spoke like this man!”
This was not a theological analysis, not a profound theory, but the most direct feeling of ordinary people:
Jesus' words are different.
His words are not knowledge but life; not religious language but words carrying authority and light; not empty doctrine but words that pierce to the depths of the heart.
The officers came to seize Jesus, but were seized by Jesus' words.
They were men carrying out orders, yet they stopped in their tracks after hearing the truth.
This shows us that words carrying the power of the Holy Spirit cannot be ignored.
Jesus did not quote others as the ordinary rabbis did; He said directly, “Truly, truly, I tell you…” His words carry heavenly authority, because He Himself is the truth.
Yet the Pharisees' reaction exposed their real problem.
They said:
“You aren’t also led astray, are you?”
They did not think about why the officers were shaken, did not ask what Jesus had actually said, did not seek the truth. Their first reaction was denial.
The proud do not first listen to the truth; they first protect their own position.
Then they said:
“Have any of the rulers believed in him, or of the Pharisees?”
This sentence exposes the deepest foundation of their faith: not God, but authority and group identity.
What they meant was:
“We who know the law do not believe, so He must be wrong.”
They made “human status” the standard of truth. But spiritual truth is never decided by majority vote or by power. God's truth is often seen by only a few.
Often what truly keeps people from believing in the Lord is not a lack of evidence but “fear of being different from the mainstream.”
Finally, verse 49 is the most chilling line of the whole passage:
“But this multitude that doesn’t know the law is cursed.”
This is religious pride at its most naked.
They looked down on the people, thinking themselves spiritual and others lowly; thinking they understood the law and others were ignorant; thinking they represented God and others were unworthy.
But the greatest irony is this: those farthest from God are often the ones who think they know God best.
They were familiar with the Scriptures yet did not know Christ; they studied the law yet rejected life; they talked about God yet opposed the Son of God.
This passage reminds us:
First, Jesus' words are unlike all other words in the world. His words carry life, authority, and the power of the Holy Spirit.
Second, truth can seize the most ordinary people. The officers had no theological training, yet they were closer to the truth than the religious leaders.
Third, the proud find it hard to receive the truth, because what they protect first is not God but their own position.
Fourth, do not make human status the standard of truth. True truth comes from God, not from group pressure.
Fifth, religious pride makes people look down on others and blinds them to themselves. The more truly God's people know God, the more humble they become.
q: When Jesus' words shine on you, are you moved like the officers, or do you first protect your position like the Pharisees?
Are you willing today to lay down your pride and simply let the Lord's words take hold of your heart?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, make our hearts like those officers, willing to be touched by Your words, and not blinded by pride like the Pharisees. Remove from us the self-righteous heart that thinks it already knows, and bring us simply and humbly to Jesus. May Your words take hold of us every day, so that our lives are renewed by the truth. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Nicodemus (he who came to him by night, being one of them) said to them,
“Does our law judge a man, unless it first hears from him personally and knows what he does?”
They answered him, “Are you also from Galilee? Search, and see that no prophet has arisen out of Galilee.”
Everyone went to his own house,
b: Though this passage is short, it is a deeply profound picture of the human heart. In the midst of hostility, accusation, and emotion, Nicodemus stood up, faintly but bravely, and spoke a word of fairness for Jesus. This passage shows us that even in the deepest darkness, there are still people willing to draw near to the truth; but when people are ruled by pride, even the law itself can be used to reject the truth.
The text begins by mentioning:
“Nicodemus (he who came to him by night, being one of them).”

This reminds us of the story in John 3. At that time Nicodemus was the one who came to Jesus secretly at night. He had a longing but did not dare to be open; he had questions but did not yet fully believe; his heart was drawn to Jesus, yet he still lived under the eyes of others and religious pressure.
Now, in chapter 7, he begins to change.
He did not at once declare publicly, “Jesus is the Christ.” But he was willing to stand up and speak a word of justice. In that setting, this was already a great step.
He said:
“Does our law judge a man, unless it first hears from him personally and knows what he does?”
Nicodemus did not directly defend Jesus; he simply returned to the most basic fairness:
“Shouldn’t we first hear Him?”
This sentence seems simple, but it shines a light on the Pharisees' hypocrisy.
They lifted up the law every day, yet were unwilling to keep even its most basic justice. They talked of fairness with their mouths, while in their hearts they had already condemned Jesus.
This is the most terrifying thing about religious pride: people use truth to oppose truth, and use the law to oppose God.
Nicodemus reminded them that the true law is fair, and true truth has no foregone conclusions.
Yet the Pharisees' reaction was very real:
“Are you also from Galilee?”
They did not answer the question; they attacked the person. When people have no truth to stand on, they begin personal attacks.
What they meant was:
“Have you been influenced by Jesus too? Are you on His side? Have you become one of those ignorant people?”
The proud fear most that others will disagree with them, so they use shame, labels, and pressure to control the group.
Then they said again:
“Search, and see that no prophet has arisen out of Galilee.”
This statement was itself wrong. Jonah came from near Galilee, but because of emotion and prejudice they no longer cared about the truth.
This shows us:
When people reject the true light, even those who know the Scriptures well are blinded by their own prejudice.
Finally, verse 53 says:
“Everyone went to his own house.”
This sentence is quiet, yet heavy.
Jesus was not received, the truth was not taken seriously, and people dispersed with their own prejudices and positions.
Everyone went home, but the problem was not solved; the truth still stood before them, only they were unwilling to submit.
This verse also seems to remind us:
A gathering can end, a discussion can disperse, but whether a person truly responds to Jesus is the most important thing.
This passage reminds us:
First, truth is often made clear under pressure. Though Nicodemus was not yet complete, he began to be willing to stand toward the light.
Second, those who truly belong to God respect fairness and truth: no foregone conclusions, no condemning along with the crowd.
Third, the proud do not answer the truth; they attack the person, because what they are really protecting is their own position.
Fourth, being familiar with the Bible is not the same as knowing God. Without humility, even a great deal of knowledge can become blindness.
Fifth, each person must finally decide: go home and keep living their own life, or truly respond to the Jesus who stands before them.
q: When truth conflicts with group pressure, which side will you choose to stand on?
Are you willing, like Nicodemus, even if imperfectly, to begin bravely drawing near to the light?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, make us like Nicodemus: even when we are still weak, willing to draw near to the truth. Remove from us prejudice, pride, and preconceived ideas, so that we do not merely study the truth but truly submit to it. Let us not only hear Jesus but truly respond to Him. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives.
Now very early in the morning, he came again into the temple, and all the people came to him. He sat down and taught them.
The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman taken in adultery. Having set her in the middle,
they told him, “Teacher, we found this woman in adultery, in the very act.
Now in our law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. What then do you say about her?”
They said this testing him, that they might have something to accuse him of. But Jesus stooped down and wrote on the ground with his finger.
b: This passage is one of the most profound scenes in the Bible. On one side are human condemnation, shame, and entrapment; on the other are Jesus' quietness, wisdom, and mercy. And the core of the whole story is not only the woman's sin, but this: how people use another's sin to cover their own.
The text begins:
“Everyone went to his own house, but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives.”

The crowd dispersed and went back to their own lives; Jesus chose to go to the Mount of Olives. The Mount of Olives was where He often prayed and communed with the Father. This shows us that all of Jesus' power, wisdom, and love did not come from people but from His intimate relationship with the Father.
Early the next morning He came again to the temple to teach. He did not stop serving because of human hostility; He kept faithfully bringing the truth to people.
Just then a group of scribes and Pharisees brought a woman.
The text specifically says:
“Having set her in the middle.”
This was not only a legal matter but a public humiliation.
She was pushed into the center of the crowd, made the focus of all eyes, the object of accusation, a tool for religious performance.

What is even more notable: the text mentions only the woman and not the man. According to the law, both the man and the woman who committed adultery should be dealt with. But they seized only the woman. This shows that their real purpose was not justice but exploitation.
Then they said to Jesus:
“Now in our law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. What then do you say about her?”
This was a trap.
If Jesus said “forgive her,” they could accuse Him of violating the law of Moses; if Jesus said “stone her,” He would lose His image of mercy and grace.
They were not seeking truth but setting a trap. They cared nothing for the woman's life or for God's heart; they only wanted to use a person's failure to attack Jesus.
This is the darkest side of religion: using truth to hurt people, using the law to exalt oneself, using another's sin to cover one's own pride.
Yet verse 6 gives us a very quiet and very powerful picture:
“But Jesus stooped down and wrote on the ground with his finger.”
He did not answer at once, did not react with emotion, was not drawn into accusation and confusion.
He became quiet.
This quietness was not weakness but heavenly authority. He was not pulled along by their trap, because He lived in the Father's peace.
Often people push things forward with emotion, but Jesus overcame confusion with quietness. People wanted to condemn at once; Jesus paused first.
He knew that what truly needed to be dealt with was not only the woman's sin but the hearts of those holding the stones.
This passage reminds us:
First, many people are interested in sin but have no compassion for people. The Pharisees valued the law but lost love.
Second, people easily use another's failure to lift themselves up. This is pride and a self-centered life.
Third, those who truly belong to God do not rush to condemn but first come before the Father. Jesus' quietness came from His connection with the Father.
Fourth, when religion loses love, it becomes a tool for hurting people. When truth has no grace, it turns into stones.
Fifth, what Jesus sees is not only people's actions but their hearts. He knows who is truly sinning and who is pretending to be righteous.
q: Have you ever, like the Pharisees, used another person's problems to display your own rightness?
Today, are you willing to put down the stone in your hand and learn Jesus' mercy and quietness?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, guard our hearts so that we do not become people who only condemn others. Let us be like Jesus, having quietness, wisdom, and mercy that come from You. When we see the weakness of others, let us lift up grace and not stones; let us come not with proud accusation but with love and truth. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: But when they continued asking him, he looked up and said to them, “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her.”
Again he stooped down and wrote on the ground with his finger.
They, when they heard it, being convicted by their conscience, went out one by one, beginning from the oldest, even to the last. Jesus was left alone with the woman where she was, in the middle.
Jesus, standing up, saw her and said, “Woman, where are your accusers? Did no one condemn you?”
She said, “No one, Lord.” Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.”
b: This passage is one of the most beautiful pictures in the gospel. Jesus neither denies sin nor condones sin; He has both truth and grace; He lets people see their own darkness, and also gives them hope for a new beginning.
The center of the whole passage is not the woman's sin, but how Jesus treats a sinner.
The text begins:
“But when they continued asking him.”
The Pharisees would not stop, because they wanted to force Jesus to take a position. They were not seeking justice but craving condemnation. They did not want to save anyone; they only wanted to win.
So Jesus finally stood up and spoke a sentence that has echoed through the ages:
“He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her.”
Jesus did not say the woman was without sin. He acknowledged that sin is real. But He turned the focus from “others' sin” to “their own sin.”
The Pharisees thought they were the judges, but Jesus let them discover that they were sinners too.
This sentence shone like a light into every conscience.
At first everyone saw only the woman's sin; now they began to see their own. At first everyone held stones in their hands; now they began to discover that their hearts were stone too.
Then the text says:
“Again he stooped down and wrote on the ground with his finger.”
After speaking, He did not press the attack, did not humiliate, did not pile on after winning. He became quiet again.
One who truly has authority does not need to suppress people with emotion. True truth from God does not drive people to despair but wakes them up.
Then verse 9 is a most striking scene:
“Went out one by one, beginning from the oldest, even to the last.”
Why from the oldest? Because the older a person is, the more he knows the sin and darkness within himself. They had thought they stood in the light, and only now found that they too needed grace.
The stones were not thrown, because the true light had already shone into every conscience.
In the end, only two were left at the scene:
“Jesus was left alone with the woman where she was, in the middle.”
One was completely holy and truly qualified to condemn; the other was covered in shame and truly guilty.
And this is the gospel.
The truly sinless Lord stood before the truly guilty.
Then Jesus asked:
“Did no one condemn you?”
The woman said:
“No one, Lord.”
Then Jesus spoke the gentlest words of the gospel:
“Neither do I condemn you.”
This was not because she had no sin, but because Jesus would one day bear her sin for her. He was not ignoring sin; He was preparing Himself to go to the cross.
He was not saying sin does not matter, but: “I am willing to bear it for you.”
But Jesus did not stop at grace. He went on:
“Go your way. From now on, sin no more.”
True grace is not indulgence, and true love is not letting things go. Jesus forgives people so that they may be set free; Jesus accepts people so that they may change.
He did not only rescue the woman from the stones; He wanted to rescue her from sin.
This passage reminds us:
First, people easily see the sins of others but not their own. Only when the true light shines in do we truly come to know ourselves.
Second, Jesus, who is truly qualified to condemn, chose mercy. And those least qualified to condemn are often the ones who most love to condemn others.
Third, grace is not denying sin but bearing sin. Jesus did not say sin is unimportant; He was willing to pay the price for sin.
Fourth, true forgiveness brings a changed life. “Sin no more” is not a demand but a new beginning.
Fifth, the gospel is not “you have no sin,” but “you have sin, yet Jesus loves you and is willing to save you.” This is true grace.
q: Have you also held a stone in your hand, ready to condemn someone?
Today, are you willing to put down the stone and let Jesus' grace restore you again?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for not treating us according to our sins, but showing us grace in Jesus. Remove from us the proud heart that condemns others, and let us truly see our own need. Thank You, Jesus, for not condemning us and for giving us a chance to begin again. Help us turn from sin and live out a new life. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Again, therefore, Jesus spoke to them, saying, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.”
b: Though this verse is only a single sentence, it is one of the most important declarations in the whole Gospel of John. Jesus does not merely bring light; He Himself is the light. He does not teach people how to find the light; He is the one true source of light for human life.

And that this sentence comes right after the woman caught in adultery was forgiven makes it all the more profound. Jesus has just let people see human darkness, religious darkness, the darkness of pride, and the darkness of sin. Then He immediately declares:
“I am the light of the world.”
It means that what can truly solve darkness is not the law, not human effort, not religious systems, not human morality, but Jesus Himself.
He does not light up one part; He is the light of the world. Jew or Gentile, poor or rich, however dark the past, whoever is willing to come to Him can receive light.
“Light” has deep meaning in the Bible:
Light stands for truth. Light stands for life. Light stands for holiness. Light stands for God's presence. Light stands for direction. Light stands for hope.
Without light, people live in confusion; without light, people cannot tell direction; without light, people take darkness as normal; without light, people do not even know they are lost.

Today the problem for many people is not only doing wrong, but living in darkness without knowing it. People think they can see, yet are blind in spirit; people think they are free, yet are bound by sin; people think they are clear, yet their direction is completely wrong.
So Jesus did not come to “add a little light”; He came to completely change the state of a person's life.
Then He said:
“He who follows me will not walk in the darkness.”
Notice, He did not say:
“He who knows me, studies me, discusses me, admires me.”
But rather:
“He who follows me.”
Light is not for admiring but for following.
True faith does not stay at knowledge but changes the direction of life. To follow Jesus means:
No longer following ourselves; no longer following the world; no longer following the flesh; no longer following darkness.
But letting Jesus decide the direction.
Many want the light but do not want to follow; want peace but are unwilling to surrender; want blessing but still reign as their own king.
But Jesus says: the way to truly leave darkness is not just to “know the light” but to “follow the light.”
Then He promised:
“But will have the light of life.”
Not a passing light, but “the light of life.”
It means this light will enter your life. It does not only light up the outside; it changes the inside.
He will:
Light up your thinking; renew your values; change your outlook; heal your darkness; lead you on the right path; bring you out of sin and death.
The light of the world can only shine on the outside; Jesus' light can shine into the human soul.
And He does not let you shine only once in a while; He gives you a new life.
This passage reminds us:
First, Jesus does not bring light; He Himself is the light. Apart from Him, life is always in darkness.
Second, the greatest human problem is not outward difficulty but inward darkness. Only Jesus can truly light up the human heart.
Third, true faith is not admiring Jesus but following Jesus. Following means putting down our own way.
Fourth, Jesus' light is not only outward help but renewal of life. He wants to put the light of life within us.
Fifth, darkness is not what is frightening; refusing the light is. As long as we are willing to come to Jesus, even the deepest darkness can be lit up.
q: What darkness in your life have you still not let Jesus shine into?
Are you willing not only to “know” Jesus but truly to “follow” Him?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for giving us Jesus as the light of the world. Light up every dark place in our lives, so that we no longer live within ourselves but truly follow Jesus. Put the light of life within us, so that we are no longer lost but live in Your truth, peace, and life. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: The Pharisees therefore said to him, “You testify about yourself. Your testimony is not valid.”
Jesus answered them, “Even if I testify about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I came from, and where I am going; but you don’t know where I came from, or where I am going.
You judge according to the flesh. I judge no one.
Even if I do judge, my judgment is true, for I am not alone, but I am with the Father who sent me.
It’s also written in your law that the testimony of two people is valid.
I am one who testifies about myself, and the Father who sent me testifies about me.”
b: This passage is a clash between a heavenly view and an earthly view. The Pharisees saw Jesus but did not know Him; Jesus knew who He was, where He came from, and where He was going. The real difference is not outward appearance but whether a life is lived in the Father's light.
The text begins:
“The Pharisees therefore said to him, ‘You testify about yourself. Your testimony is not valid.’”
Under Jewish law, a person's testimony needed two or three witnesses to stand. The Pharisees seized on this to attack Jesus:
“You keep saying you are the light, that you are from God, that you are the Christ. This is only what you say yourself; it doesn't count.”

But in fact they were not pursuing truth but rejecting it. For Jesus had already proved who He was by His miracles, His teaching, His life, the testimony of John the Baptist, and the prophecies of Scripture.
The problem was never “insufficient evidence” but “a heart unwilling to believe.”
Then Jesus answered:
“Even if I testify about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I came from, and where I am going.”
This sentence is very important.
Jesus' assurance was not built on how people see Him but on His relationship with the Father.
He knew:
He came from the Father; He lived for the Father; He would return to the Father.
So He did not need human approval to prove Himself.
Many lives are unstable because they do not know where they came from, what they live for, or where they are going. So they desperately seek people's affirmation, status, and a sense of worth.
But Jesus was completely different. There was no insecurity in Him, because He knew who He was.
Then He said to the Pharisees:
“But you don’t know where I came from, or where I am going.”
Their greatest problem was not lack of knowledge but spiritual blindness.
They could see Jesus' outward appearance but not His source. They knew His physical background but not that He came from the Father.
This is the person of the flesh: able to look only at the outside, unable to see spiritual reality.
So Jesus went on:
“You judge according to the flesh.”
This was exactly the Pharisees' core problem.
They looked at:
Background, education, status, tradition, rules, outward things. They measured God by human standards.
They thought they were judging Jesus, but what was really revealed was their own darkness.
And Jesus said:
“I judge no one.”
This does not mean He had no discernment, but that He does not condemn by appearance, prejudice, and flesh as people do.
If He judges, His judgment is true, because He does not act on His own but is completely one with the Father.
Then He said:
“For I am not alone, but I am with the Father who sent me.”
This is the source of Jesus' strength.
He was never alone. Every word, every decision, every step of His way was walked with the Father.
A person's greatest security is not having people support him but knowing that the Father is with him.
Finally Jesus said:
“I am one who testifies about myself, and the Father who sent me testifies about me.”
How does the Father testify for Him?
Through:
The prophecies of Scripture; John the Baptist; miracles and wonders; the power of the Holy Spirit; the Father's voice from heaven; the life of Jesus Himself.
Jesus was not a lonely witness; all of heaven was testifying for Him.
This passage reminds us:
First, if people are unwilling to believe, no amount of evidence helps. The problem is not a lack of light but refusing the light.
Second, a truly stable life comes from knowing where we came from and where we are going. Jesus' assurance came from His relationship with the Father.
Third, the person of the flesh judges only by appearance. But God looks at the heart, at life, at truth.
Fourth, Jesus did not act on His own; He was always with the Father. This is also the source of His power and peace.
Fifth, if we live in the Father's presence, we do not need the world to prove ourselves. For true worth comes from God's affirmation.
q: Is your sense of worth built on how people see you or on how the Heavenly Father sees you?
Are you willing, like Jesus, to stop judging by appearance and live in the Father's eyes?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, let us no longer live under the eyes and approval of people, but like Jesus know that we came from You and will return to You. Remove from us the heart that judges people by appearance, and teach us to see people, things, and ourselves with Your eyes. And let us live every day in Your presence, no longer lonely, no longer insecure. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: They said therefore to him, “Where is your Father?” Jesus answered, “You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also.”
Jesus spoke these words in the treasury, as he taught in the temple. Yet no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come.
b: Though this passage is short, it opens up a very deep truth: if people do not know Jesus, they cannot truly know the Father; and those who truly know Jesus enter into a relationship with the Father.
The Pharisees heard Jesus keep mentioning “the Father,” so they asked Him:
“Where is your Father?”
They thought Jesus was talking about an earthly father, or demanding that He produce a “witness.” But in fact Jesus was speaking of the Heavenly Father.
This once again shows that people of the flesh can only understand the earthly level and cannot enter spiritual truth.
They stood face to face with Jesus yet had no idea what He was talking about. This is the deepest spiritual blindness.
So Jesus answered:
“You know neither me nor my Father.”
This sentence directly exposed the Pharisees' true condition.
They considered themselves to know God best; they knew the law well; they were in the temple every day; they studied the Scriptures; they led the people; yet Jesus told them directly:
“You don't know the Father at all.”
How startling!
It turns out:
Understanding religion is not knowing God; knowing Bible facts is not knowing the Father; having a spiritual appearance is not having a relationship with God.
The only way to truly know the Father is Jesus.
So He went on:
“If you knew me, you would know my Father also.”
Jesus does not merely introduce the Father; He is the revelation of the Father. He does not bring a portion of information about God; He is the radiance of God's glory.
To see Jesus' love is to see the Father's love; to see Jesus' compassion is to see the Father's compassion; to see Jesus' truth is to see the Father's truth.
So apart from Jesus, people can only stay within religion and cannot truly enter a relationship with the Father.

This is also the problem for many today: they know a lot about God but do not know God's heart. They can talk theology but do not understand the Father's love. They can serve but are not close to the Lord.
For true life is not accumulating knowledge but being joined to Jesus.
Then verse 20 says:
“Jesus spoke these words in the treasury, as he taught in the temple.”
The treasury was a place in the temple where many people gathered, which means Jesus spoke these words in public. He did not say them in private or secretly, but openly declared the truth.
He did not fear human hostility, because He lived completely in the Father's will.
The last sentence is important:
“Yet no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come.”
This statement is repeated again and again in John.
People wanted to seize Him but could not; people wanted to kill Him but could not lay hands on Him.
Because Jesus was not living in human hands but in the Father's timing.
The one who truly governed His life was not His enemies but the Heavenly Father.
This is a great comfort for us:
If we live in God's will, our lives are not in the hands of circumstances, not in the hands of human malice, not in the hands of Satan, but in the Father's hands.
Nothing can come to us ahead of God's permission.
This passage reminds us:
First, those who do not know Jesus cannot truly know the Father. Jesus is the only way to the Father.
Second, religious knowledge is not a life relationship. To truly know God is through being joined to Jesus.
Third, Jesus is the fullest revelation of the Father. To see Him is to see the Father's heart.
Fourth, Jesus did not live under human control but in the Father's timing. This is the source of His true peace and authority.
Fifth, those who truly belong to God can also live securely in a chaotic world, because they know the Father governs all.
q: Does your knowledge of God stay at the level of facts, or have you truly built a relationship with Jesus?
Today, are you willing to know Jesus more deeply so that you may truly know the Heavenly Father?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for revealing Yourself to us through Jesus. Let us not stay within religious knowledge but truly know Your heart. Help us to be joined to Jesus more deeply every day, so that we become more and more like Him. And teach us to rest in Your sovereignty, believing that our lives are in Your hands. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: Jesus said therefore again to them, “I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sins. Where I go, you can’t come.”
The Jews therefore said, “Will he kill himself, because he says, ‘Where I am going, you can’t come’?”
He said to them, “You are from beneath. I am from above. You are of this world. I am not of this world.
I said therefore to you that you will die in your sins; for unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins.”
b: This passage is a very solemn warning from Jesus. He does not only point out the human problem; He also points out the final outcome if people reject Him.
And the core of the whole passage is a single sentence:
“Unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins.”
This is not a threat but the truth.
Jesus first said:
“I am going away, and you will seek me.”
He once again foretold that He would leave the world and return to the Father. But He said that one day people would want to find Him and not be able to.
What heavy words these are.
Today people can ignore Jesus, push Him away, or put off responding to Him, but one day they will find that at the moment they truly need Him, they are the ones who rejected Him.
Then He said:
“You will die in your sins.”
This sentence is extremely solemn.
The greatest human problem is not circumstances, not pain, not lack, not failure, but sin.
Sin separates people from God; sin makes people live in darkness; sin keeps people from entering eternal life; sin makes people dead inside even while they are alive.
And the most terrible thing is that if people reject Jesus, there is no way for sins to be forgiven.
“Dying in sins” is not only physical death but eternal separation from God.
Yet the Jews' reaction once again showed their spiritual blindness.
They said:
“Will he kill himself?”
Jesus spoke of heavenly things, and they understood only with earthly thinking.
This is exactly the mark of people of the world: able to understand only earthly things, unable to grasp spiritual things.
So Jesus directly pointed out the fundamental difference:
“You are from beneath. I am from above. You are of this world. I am not of this world.”
This is not about geography but about the source of life.
“From beneath” means: of the flesh, of the world, of sin, of darkness, of self.
“From above” means: of God, of truth, of the Holy Spirit, of the kingdom of heaven.
Jesus was saying: the reason you do not understand me is not that I am unclear, but that your life still belongs to this world.
People of the world live by the logic of the world; people of God live by God's truth.
This is also why, without being born again, a person cannot truly understand God.
Finally, Jesus repeated:
“Unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins.”
Notice, He said “die in your sins” twice.
Because this is the most fundamental human problem.
It is not that religion is insufficient, not that self-cultivation is insufficient, not that effort is insufficient, but that people need salvation.
And the key to salvation is not works but faith.
Believe what?
Believe that “Jesus is the Christ.” That is:
He is the Son of God; He is the Savior; He is the only way; He can forgive sins; He can give life; He can bring people from death into eternal life.
Those who reject Him do not lack religion; they lack life.
This passage reminds us:
First, the greatest human problem is not circumstances but sin. Sin separates people from God and makes them live in death.
Second, Jesus is the only one who can solve sin. Apart from Him, people cannot truly receive life.
Third, people of the world cannot understand heavenly truth. Only those who are born again can enter the kingdom of God.
Fourth, not believing in Jesus is not just lacking one religious option, but still dying in sin.
Fifth, the key to true salvation is this: do you believe that Jesus is the Christ?
q: Do you truly believe that Jesus is not only a teacher but the Christ, the Savior?
Is the way you live now more like a person of the world or a person of the kingdom of heaven?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for sending Jesus to save us from sin and death. Open our eyes, so that we no longer live in the darkness of the world but truly believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Savior, the Lord of life. Set us free from sin, bring us from death into eternal life, and let us live out a heavenly life. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, amen.
